episodes.text: Father called Crusoe into his chamber and delivered a long, tearful plea against going to sea, urging the virtues of the middle station of life.
Crusoe was briefly moved by his father's counsel and resolved to stay home, but within a few days the resolution faded.
Crusoe appealed to his mother to intercede with his father for consent to one sea voyage; she refused and scolded him.
On 1 September 1651, without parental consent or blessing, Crusoe boarded a ship at Hull bound for London — his first voyage to sea.
A fierce storm struck almost immediately after leaving the Humber; Crusoe was terrified and desperately sea-sick, vowing to return home if spared.
When the storm abated and the sea calmed, a companion plied Crusoe with punch; within five or six days he had entirely forgotten his repentance and resolutions.
A second, far worse storm struck at Yarmouth Roads on the eighth day at anchor, terrifying even the master and seamen.

The ship's masts were cut away in the storm; she sprang a leak with four feet of water in the hold, and eventually foundered; all crew escaped in a rescue boat and got safe ashore at Winterton Ness, walking to Yarmouth.
At Yarmouth the survivors were treated humanely by magistrates and merchants, given money to go to London or Hull.

The ship captain (master's role) earnestly urged Crusoe never to go to sea again, calling the wreck a visible hand of Heaven against him and predicting disasters until his father's words were fulfilled.
Despite multiple warnings, Crusoe chose not to return to Hull but instead travelled to London by land, still undecided whether to go home or to sea.
Shame at the neighbours' laughter prevented Crusoe from returning home after the wreck; the memory of distress faded and he eventually looked out for a new voyage.
Crusoe sailed to the Guinea coast with an honest captain who befriended him, directing him to invest £40 in toys and trifles; the voyage was a success.
Crusoe returned from Guinea with five pounds nine ounces of gold-dust, which sold in London for almost £300 — his only fully successful voyage.
The Guinea captain died shortly after returning; Crusoe resolved to make the same voyage again under the former mate.
On the second Guinea voyage, Crusoe's ship was seized by a Turkish (Moorish) rover from Sallee; three men were killed, eight wounded, and the crew were taken prisoner.
Crusoe was kept by the captain of the Moorish rover as his personal slave, while the rest of the crew were sent to the emperor's court; he spent about two years in slavery at Sallee.

Crusoe seized the opportunity when his Moorish master's guests cancelled a fishing trip; he loaded the longboat with provisions, powder, shot, tools, and wax while deceiving the Moor Ismael into fetching more supplies.
Crusoe tossed the Moor Ismael overboard a league from shore and threatened him with a fowling-piece; Ismael swam back to shore unharmed.
Crusoe kept the boy Xury aboard after extracting an oath of faithfulness on pain of being thrown overboard; Xury swore and proved willing.
Crusoe sailed south from Sallee, covering about 150 miles in the first day-and-a-half, steering to hug the African coast and avoid the Emperor of Morocco's territory.
After five days' sailing the wind shifted; Crusoe anchored at the mouth of an unknown river on the African coast where wild animals howled all night; they did not go ashore.
Near the African coast, a creature (possibly a lion) swam toward the anchored boat at night; Crusoe shot at it and it turned back.
Xury volunteered to go ashore for water alone, saying 'If wild mans come, they eat me, you go wey' — his selflessness made Crusoe love him.
Xury went ashore, shot a hare-like animal, and found fresh water; they feasted and refilled their jars.
Crusoe shot a sleeping lion on a hillock — breaking its leg with the first shot, hitting its head with the second; Xury swam ashore and administered the final shot.
Crusoe and Xury spent a full day skinning the lion; the hide was dried on the cabin roof and later served as Crusoe's mattress.

After the lion stop, they sailed south for ten to twelve days on sparse provisions, aiming to reach the Gambia or Senegal and find a European ship — Crusoe staked everything on meeting one or perishing.
Encountered unarmed African coastal people who exchanged dried meat and corn for goodwill; Crusoe shot a leopard that terrified them, earning their admiration and gratitude.
The African villagers gave water and provisions freely after the leopard kill; Crusoe took the leopard skin and departed after eleven more days sailing.
Rounded Cape de Verde, spotted it and the Cape de Verde Islands from the sea while in the longboat.
Xury spotted a Portuguese ship; Crusoe signalled distress with his patron's flag and a gun shot, and the ship hove to and took him aboard.
A Scotch sailor aboard the Portuguese ship translated; Crusoe was received with all his goods and told his goods would be kept safe until Brazil.
The Portuguese captain refused any payment for the rescue, citing charity and the principle that he might one day need the same; promised to carry Crusoe to Brazil.
Portuguese captain sold Xury to himself for 60 pieces of eight, with a written obligation to free Xury in ten years if he turned Christian; Crusoe reluctantly agreed.
Arrived at All Saints' Bay, Brazil, about twenty-two days after departing the rescue point; received all goods and about 220 pieces of eight total from the captain for cargo, skins, and boat.
Obtained a letter of naturalisation in Brazil, purchased uncured land, and formed a plantation plan, intending to retrieve £100 of his London money.
Gave the Portuguese captain letters and a procuration to retrieve £100 sterling from his money in London via the English captain's widow.

The Portuguese captain, on reaching Lisbon, arranged through English merchants to send the full £100 in English plantation goods to Brazil, including tools and ironwork Crusoe had not thought to order.
With the English-goods cargo, Crusoe sold them at great advantage, bought a Negro slave and a European servant, and quadrupled the value of his investment.
The following year Crusoe raised fifty great rolls of tobacco on his plantation, laid by for the Lisbon fleet; his wealth and ambition were growing.
After nearly four years in Brazil, three merchant partners proposed a secret Guinea slave-trading voyage; Crusoe agreed to go as supercargo, abandoning his prospering plantation.
Made a formal will before departing, naming the Portuguese captain as universal heir of the plantation and directing half the produce to him and half shipped to England.
Sailed from Brazil on 1 September 1659 — exactly eight years after leaving Hull — as supercargo on a 120-ton ship carrying six guns and fourteen men plus master and his boy.
A violent tornado struck the ship for twelve days; one man died of calenture, one man and the boy were washed overboard; ship ended up near the Guiana coast well west of Africa.
After the storm, master and Crusoe resolved to sail for Barbados rather than return to Brazil, as the ship was leaky and disabled.
A second storm drove the ship westward; it struck a sandbank and the sea broke over it; crew expecting immediate wreck, sheltering in close quarters.
Ship stuck fast on the sandbank; the first boat was staved and lost; eleven men got into the second boat and pushed off into a violent sea.
A great wave overturned the longboat and separated the crew; all were swallowed in the surf — Crusoe alone survived.
Crusoe was carried through the surf repeatedly, struck against a rock with great force, but clung on and finally clambered up the cliff to dry ground.
Reached the mainland safely; sat on the grass above the waves thanking God; found all crewmates drowned — none survived but himself.
After the joy of survival abated, took stock: wet, no clothes, no food, no weapons — only a knife, a tobacco-pipe, and a little tobacco; feared wild beasts as night fell.
First night ashore: climbed a thorny fir-like tree for safety, found fresh water nearby, slept with a cut stick for defence.
Next morning the ship had been lifted off the sandbank by the tide and driven closer to shore; Crusoe saw the overturned longboat about two miles away but a half-mile inlet blocked access.
Swam to the stranded ship at low tide; climbed in via a hanging rope; found provisions dry and untouched — ate biscuit and drank rum.
Built a raft from spare yards and spars, using a carpenter's saw to cut a topmast into lengths; loaded it with three chests of provisions, tools, arms, and powder.
Guided the laden raft toward shore using the tidal current into a creek or river inlet.
Landed the first raft safely at a small cove by waiting for high tide and mooring it with broken oars; brought all cargo ashore.
Climbed a hill and confirmed his fate: he was on an island, entirely surrounded by sea, barren and uninhabited except by wild birds and beasts.

Made a second raft voyage to the wreck and salvaged nails, spikes, a screw-jack, hatchets, grindstone, iron crows, two barrels of musket bullets, seven muskets, a fowling-piece, powder, sheet-lead, all remaining men's clothes, a fore-topsail, a hammock, and bedding.
Set up a tent from the sail and poles, piled chests and casks in a circle as a fortification, and slept inside with pistols at his head — first proper night's rest on the island.

Made five or six raft salvage voyages over thirteen days on shore, retrieving rigging, ropes, canvas, sails, cables, ironwork, hogshead of bread, three runlets of rum, box of sugar, barrel of flour, razors, scissors, knives, forks, and about thirty-six pounds in mixed coin.
On the final raft load the raft overturned in the cove, losing much of the iron and requiring exhausting labour to recover what could be salvaged from the water.
Swam back from the ship as a storm rose; the following morning the wrecked ship had vanished entirely, broken up overnight.

Resolved to move camp from the low marshy ground near shore and chose a new site on the N.N.W. side of a rising hill with a hollow in the rock face, a small green plain, shade from the sun, and a view to the sea.
Built a fortified palisade enclosure at the new hillside camp: two rows of sharp stakes five and a half feet tall, cable laid between them, no door — only a ladder lifted over after entry.

Moved all provisions and goods into the palisade enclosure, erected a double tent with inner and outer layers covered by tarpaulin, and began sleeping in the mate's hammock rather than the bed brought from the ship.
Dug a cave behind the tent into the rock, hauling earth and stones out through the tent to raise the ground inside the enclosure; the cave served as a cellar-store.

A lightning strike during a storm triggered sudden terror about the powder supply; suspended all building work and spent a fortnight separating roughly 240 pounds of powder into approximately 100 small parcels hidden in rocks and caves to prevent a single ignition destroying it all.
First hunting expedition on the island: discovered goats; shot a she-goat, whose kid followed him to the enclosure; attempted to tame the kid but it would not eat and was killed for food.
Cut a large wooden post into a cross and inscribed 'I came on shore here on the 30th September 1659' — erected on the landing beach to mark the date and track the passage of time.

Fell into deep despair, weeping about his desolate condition and questioning Providence; then reasoned himself back from the brink by counting what he had versus what he could have lost — arrived at a cautious gratitude.
Devised a calendar post: daily notches, longer notch every seventh day, longest notch for each new month — kept weekly, monthly, and yearly reckoning of time.

Itemised salvaged goods previously unrecorded: pens, ink, paper, compasses, mathematical instruments, charts, navigation books, three English Bibles, Portuguese books, prayer-books, and other books — all carefully secured.
The ship's dog swam ashore the day after the first cargo and became a trusty companion for many years; both cats were also brought ashore.

Wrote up a formal 'debtor and creditor' account of his condition — evil against good — and concluded there was always something to be thankful for even in the worst case; helped master his despondency.
Enlarged the cave sideways to the right and then out through the rock, creating a back door through the palisade to a separate storehouse area.
Built a table and chair from ship's planks — first items of furniture; then added shelves along the cave wall to organise all tools, nails, and ironwork.
Added a turf wall two feet thick outside the palisade; later raised rafters and thatched the roof with branches to keep out rain.

Began keeping a journal of daily employment; describes initial landing day terror: vomiting seawater, running about wringing hands, crying 'undone, undone', collapsing exhausted — first night slept in a tree.
Named the island 'The Island of Despair' in his journal entry for 30 September 1659.
Journal confirms the salvage timeline: 1–24 October spent on multiple raft voyages to the ship; 20 October raft overturned in shoal water, most goods recovered; 25 October ship broke up in a storm.
From 26 October: marked out and began fortifying the hillside campsite; 26–30 October carried all goods to new location.
4 November: established a daily routine — gun walk 2–3 hours, work until 11, eat, sleep 12–2 (heat), work again in evening.
5 November: shot a wild cat — kept the skin; first sighting of seals on the shore.
13 November: thunder and lightning frightened him for the powder; resolved immediately to separate it into small parcels.
14–16 November: made small square boxes each holding about 1–2 lb of powder to store it dispersed.
17 November: began digging into the rock behind the tent to enlarge the cave; lacked pickaxe, shovel, and wheelbarrow.
18 November: found iron-tree wood and laboriously shaped it into a wooden shovel — the first improvised tool made on the island.
Unable to make a basket or wheelbarrow; fashioned a mortar-hod instead and used it with the wooden shovel to carry excavated earth from the cave — four days of tool-making total.
From 23 November: spent eighteen days widening and deepening the cave to serve as warehouse, kitchen, dining-room, and cellar.
10 December: cave roof collapsed on one side — a near-fatal fall of earth; spent a week propping the ceiling with posts and boards and using the posts as internal partitions.
17–20 December: fitted shelves and nails in the cave; carried everything in and set up a dresser board for victuals; made a second table.

27 December: killed a young goat and lamed another; splinted the lame one's broken leg — it healed fully and grew tame, grazing on the green by the door; first thought of breeding tame animals for food.
3 January to 14 April: built the main perimeter wall — a half-circle of about twenty-four yards, backed with a turf wall, so well disguised that the habitation would be invisible from the shore.
Tamed wild pigeons found nesting in rock holes — raised young ones but they flew away when grown; continued gathering squabs from nests for food.
Made a clay lamp from goat tallow and oakum wick — baked the clay dish in the sun; gave dim light at night since no candles available.

Shook husks from a salvaged grain bag under the rock near the fortification; about a month later discovered ten to twelve stalks of green European barley growing there — initially mistook it for a miracle of Providence.

Realised the barley sprouted from a salvaged chicken-feed bag — not a miracle; religious fervour cooled, though he acknowledged it was still remarkable providence that any grain survived the rats and landed in ideal shade.

Carefully harvested barley and rice ears (about 10–12 barley stalks and 20–30 rice stalks) at end of June; resolved to sow all of it to build a bread supply — but lost the first sowing by planting just before the dry season.
16 April: finished the ladder for the camp wall, completing the enclosure — no door visible from outside, entry and exit only by ladder over the top.

17 April: a severe earthquake struck — three shocks eight minutes apart; the cave cracked, a large rock near the sea fell, and the sea itself was violently disturbed; Crusoe fled over the wall in terror.
The earthquake was followed by a three-hour hurricane that tore up trees and covered the shore in foam; Crusoe sat outside terrified for hours before venturing back inside.
After the earthquake Crusoe was forced to cut a drainage hole through the fortification to prevent his cave from flooding in the heavy rain.
Resolved on 21 April to stay in the cave temporarily while building a second open-ground camp as an earthquake-safe alternative; feared being buried alive if island shook again.
Invented a foot-powered wheel to turn the grindstone, freeing both hands — took a full week to build and worked well.
Reduced himself to one biscuit cake a day after surveying dwindling bread supplies — made his heart very heavy.
Found a barrel of gunpowder washed ashore from the wreck, but the powder had taken water and caked solid — rolled it further up the beach.
The earthquake had heaved the wreck's forecastle six feet and broke the stern loose — the ship now accessible at low tide without swimming.

Worked the wreck daily from May 3 to June 15: cut beams with saw, wrenched planks with an iron crow, recovered fir planks, iron bolts, seamen's chests, and nearly a hundredweight of sheet lead — enough timber and ironwork to have built a boat.
On 16 June found a large turtle on the shore — the first seen; cooked it on the 17th and found sixty eggs inside; the flesh was the most savoury he had tasted since landing.
Fell gravely ill from 19 June onward: violent fever, ague, headache, chills, shivering — seven-hour ague fit on 25 June left him too weak to stand or fetch water.
During the worst of the fever on 27 June prayed aloud to God for the first time since the storm off Hull, lying helpless and crying 'Lord, look upon me!' — confused and ignorant of formal prayer.
In feverish sleep had a terrifying dream of a blazing man descending from a black cloud with a spear, declaring 'thou shalt die' for want of repentance.

Awoke from the fever-dream and reflected that eight years of seafaring wickedness had entirely extinguished his father's religious instruction — conscience had slept through every danger, deliverance, and disaster until the fever.
On June 28, recovering from the ague fit, prepared water-and-rum for the next attack, broiled goat flesh, and ate three roasted turtle eggs — the first meal over which he ever asked God's blessing.
Sitting weak by the sea on June 28, spontaneously reasoned from the earth and creatures to a Creator who must guide and govern all things — his first unprompted theological reflection.
Reasoning from providence to guilt, conscience silenced every complaint by listing the deliverances he had squandered — struck dumb, he returned to his retreat pensive and sad.
Found a roll of cured tobacco in the chest alongside the Bible; tried chewing it, steeping it in rum, and burning it over coals — used all three methods against the fever.
Opening the Bible by chance read 'Call on Me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver thee' — the words made a lasting impression though deliverance seemed remote.
For the first time in his life, knelt down and prayed to God to fulfil the promise of deliverance; then drank the tobacco-rum and slept nearly two days straight — awoke recovered and cheerful.
Fever fit entirely missed on 3 July; recovering strength, recognised he had been delivered from sickness but had not thanked God — immediately knelt and gave thanks aloud.

On 4 July began reading the New Testament every morning and evening; soon moved to pray earnestly for repentance; read 'He is exalted a Prince and a Saviour to give repentance' — threw down the book in ecstatic joy crying 'Jesus, give me repentance!'
Reinterpreted 'I will deliver thee' as deliverance from guilt rather than from the island — concluded that freedom from sin mattered more than freedom from solitude; peace of mind greatly eased.
From 4 to 14 July convalesced by walking short distances with gun; learned that going out in rainy-season storms was the worst thing for health.
On 15 July began a systematic survey of the island interior: followed the creek upstream, found savannahs, wild tobacco, aloes, and imperfect sugar cane — no cassava found.

On 16 July found melons on the ground and grapes on the trees in prime ripeness in the wooded valley; also cocoa, orange, lemon, and citron trees; gathered limes and resolved to return with bags for grapes.
Spent first night away from camp sleeping in a tree — three days' exploration total; brought home limes but grapes crushed on the way.
Returned on 19 July to find the grape heap trodden, spread about, and devoured by unknown wild creatures — resolved to dry grapes on tree branches instead.
Decided not to relocate to the interior valley — staying near the shore keeps open the possibility of rescue; built a bower in the valley as a country retreat instead.
Collected over two hundred bunches of dried raisins from tree branches on 3 August before the rains began — raisins stored as principal winter food.
Cat who had disappeared returned at end of August with three kittens — apparently mated with a wild cat; kittens were of house-breed, not wild kind.
Extended the cave through the hill to create a back door out beyond the perimeter wall — eased movement in and out of camp but felt more exposed.

On 30 September (first anniversary of landing) kept a solemn fast: prostrated himself, confessed sins, prayed for mercy through Jesus Christ — ate only a biscuit cake and bunch of grapes after sundown.
After the anniversary count set aside every seventh day as Sabbath — the first regular Sabbath observance; noted the calendar was a day or two short in reckoning.
Second grain sowing (two-thirds of seed) failed entirely — dry months followed with no rain; remainder sown in February near the bower succeeded well in March-April rains.
Discovered that the bower's living stakes had sprouted into trees forming a complete shaded canopy; pruned and shaped them, then cut a double row of living-stake hedge around his main camp wall.
Mastered basket-making from childhood memory of watching basket-makers in York; cut pliable living-stake twigs and made many wicker baskets for carrying earth and storing grain.
Travelled across to the west shore of the island with gun, dog, and rations; saw distant high land to the W/WSW — estimated 15-20 leagues off, likely Spanish or savage coast of South America.

West side of island found to be far pleasanter than his side: open savannahs with flowers, fine woods, parrots, hares, foxes — shore covered with innumerable turtles compared to three seen in eighteen months on his side.
Caught a young parrot by knocking it down with a stick; brought it home and eventually taught it to call him by name.
Completed the west-shore journey and set a marker pole on the shore; resolved to next explore the east side and return to his post.

Got lost returning from the western expedition — descended into a large hill-ringed valley, lost the sun in hazy weather for three or four days, and had to find the seaside and his post-cross before retracing his outward route home.
Dog flushed and seized a young kid on the return journey; caught it alive, made a rope-yarn collar, and penned it at the bower before heading home after an absence of over a month.
Kid nearly starved in the bower pen while he rested a week at home; went back, fed it boughs and shrubs, and led it to the main camp where it became fully tame and a devoted domestic animal.
Kept the second anniversary of landing, 30 September, as a solemn day of humble and thankful acknowledgment, now two full years on the island.

Opened the Bible to 'I will never, never leave thee, nor forsake thee' on a sad morning and was struck that the words were directed personally to him; resolved that God's favour outweighs any worldly loss.
Began the third year on the island with a settled daily division: scripture three times a day, morning gun walk, food preparation, and evening work — seldom idle.
Spent forty-two days making a single cave shelf-board for want of tools, help, and skill — work that two sawyers with a saw-pit could have done in half a day.

Cut down a large tree and hewed a single wide shelf-board from it by hand over forty-two days — three days felling, two days trimming, then days of hacking to reduce to a smooth plank about three inches thick.
First barley and rice crop threatened by goats and island hares eating the blades; fenced the crop with a hedge in three weeks and set the dog as night-guard at the gate — pests abandoned the field.
Birds descended on the ripening corn in the ear; shot three and hanged them in chains as scarecrows — birds forsook the entire area for as long as the scarecrows hung.

Reaped the first successful harvest in late December using a cutlass blade as improvised sickle and a basket; from a half-peck of seed obtained roughly two bushels of rice and two and a half bushels of barley.
Resolved not to eat any of the first harvest but to save it all as seed-corn, and to spend the next six months building the implements needed to mill and bake it.
Prepared a second larger plot (over an acre), sowed a full second season, fenced it with a hedge of his own living stakes — work took three months, partly due to the wet season.
Taught the parrot to say 'Poll' — the first word spoken on the island by any mouth but his own; talked to it constantly while working indoors during rain.
Resolved to make earthen pottery vessels from island clay, dried in the sun, to solve the vessel shortage for storing meal and dry goods.

Spent about two months attempting to make large clay pots; most cracked, fell apart, or collapsed — managed only two ugly but serviceable large vessels, which he cradled in wicker baskets for dry storage.

Discovered by accident that earthenware burned in a cooking fire became hard as stone; built a pile of pipkins and pots and maintained a fire around them all night, producing three good pipkins and two pots, one glazed by the sand melting.
Boiled meat in the new fire-hardened pot immediately — first successful cooking vessel; made broth from a piece of kid.

Unable to find suitable rock for a stone mortar; carved a wooden mortar from a hard-wood block using axe, hatchet, and fire (Indian canoe method), then made an iron-wood pestle — set aside for the next harvest.
Made three sieves from pieces of calico and muslin neckcloths salvaged from seamen's chests — solved the meal-sifting problem for several years.

Built an improvised oven: broad shallow earthen dishes fired in the kiln, a tile-paved hearth of his own baking, and an inverted pot over the loaves surrounded by embers — baked barley loaves and rice cakes successfully.
Second corn harvest yielded about twenty bushels of barley and as much or more rice — now enough to eat freely and resolved to sow only once a year.
Resolved to sow the same quantity of barley and rice every year — the forty-bushel total was sufficient for bread but not much more; annual sowing fixed at that scale.
Found the ship's boat upturned against a sand ridge, still intact; spent three or four weeks trying to right it with levers, rollers, and digging — finally gave up as impossible alone.

Conceived the idea of building a large cedar-tree canoe (periagua) and began work — spent twenty days felling the tree, fourteen days trimming branches, a month shaping the hull, and three months hollowing it out, producing a canoe large enough for twenty-six men.

When the canoe was finished, discovered it could not be moved the hundred yards to water — tried digging a declivity and then planning a canal but calculated the canal would take ten to twelve years alone; abandoned the project with great reluctance.

Completed the fourth year on the island; kept the anniversary with the same devotion as before, and noted that by constant scripture study his view of the world had shifted — the world now seemed a remote place he had left behind.

Reached a settled inner contentment: reflected that he possessed everything he could use — food, timber, grain, fruit — while his £36 coin and all surplus were worthless; understood by experience that worldly goods are only valuable in use.
Gave extended thanks for Providence having cast the ship close enough to shore to be salvaged — reasoned that without those tools, weapons, and powder he would have perished or lived as a savage.

Reflected on the void wickedness of his pre-island life: the seafaring company had laughed out what little religion his parents instilled; he had never once said 'Thank God' through Sallee, rescue, Brazil, or any earlier deliverance.
After long months of terrible reflections on his past, worked his mind to a sincere thankfulness — took his continued life as evidence his repentance was accepted; resolved never to repine again.

Noted a remarkable concurrence of dates: the same calendar day he left home for Hull he was enslaved at Sallee; the same day-of-year he escaped the Yarmouth wreck he escaped Sallee; and 30 September — his birthday — was the day he was cast ashore on the island.
Ink finally exhausted — eked it out with water until too pale to leave a mark; resolved to record only the most remarkable events.
Ship's biscuit supply long exhausted — went nearly a year without any bread before his own corn crop came in.

Clothes worn to rags; improvised waistcoats from seamen's watch-coats and eventually made a full goatskin suit — waistcoat, open-kneed breeches — plus a rain-shedding goatskin cap; acknowledged the tailoring was wretched.
Built a collapsible skin-covered umbrella after many failures — the main challenge was making it fold; it shed rain like a penthouse and blocked sun better than going without in the hottest weather.
Over approximately five uneventful years built a second, smaller canoe and dug a canal nearly half a mile to float it out to the creek — near two years of labour.
Concluded the small periagua was too small to attempt the forty-mile crossing to the mainland; abandoned the escape-by-sea plan and turned attention instead to sailing round the island.
Fitted the small canoe with a mast, sails cut from salvaged ship's canvas, lockers at each end for dry storage, and a covered gun-slot — ready for a circuit of the island.
Set out on the island circumnavigation cruise on 6 November in the sixth year, victualled with barley-bread, parched rice, rum, half a goat, powder, shot, and two watch-coats.
Reached the east side of the island and found a great ledge of rocks extending two leagues into the sea, plus a sand shoal half a league beyond — forced to go far out to sea to double the point.
Was swept two leagues out to sea by a furious current rounding the east point — paddled helplessly, feared irrecoverable loss into the open ocean, and despaired of survival.
Caught a breeze from SSE around noon, set mast and sail, and used a rock-caused eddy to the north-west to claw back toward the island.
Returned to the island's northern shore around four in the evening after the eddy spent itself, navigating calm water the last mile to land.
On reaching shore after the ocean ordeal, fell on his knees and gave God thanks for deliverance, resolving to abandon all thought of escape by boat.
Found a safe harbour for the canoe in a bay about three miles along the north shore, stowed the boat there, and marched home to the bower on foot.
Woke at the bower in a fright at a voice calling 'Robin Crusoe' — found it was Poll the parrot, who had followed him there and greeted him with his own taught phrases.
Decided to leave the canoe on the north shore rather than risk the east-point currents again — effectively resigned to being without a boat on his usual side of the island.
Spent about a year in a sedate, settled life — improved his earthenware by making a potter's wheel, made wicker baskets, and fashioned a clay tobacco-pipe.

In the eleventh year, as powder ran low, set snares and pitfall traps for goats — traps sprung but empty or broken; eventually caught one large old he-goat and three kids (one male, two female) in a single night.
Released the old trapped he-goat (could not safely handle him), brought the three kids home, tethered them in the new enclosure, and hand-fed them barley and rice until tame.
Began a goat enclosure — started with a two-mile perimeter, then saw the folly and scaled back to 150 yards by 100 yards; took about three months to hedge it in.
Within about a year and a half of the enclosure's completion had a flock of roughly twelve goats; within two more years the herd had grown to forty-three, plus kills for food.
Set up a dairy — collecting a gallon or two of milk a day, and teaching himself to make butter, cheese, and salt.

Described the household dinner scene: himself as monarch, Poll on his finger, old dog at his right hand, two preserved tame cats on either side — the original two cats long dead and buried by his own hand.

Walked to the east-point hill to reconnoitre the currents, dressed in full goatskin kit — cap, short jacket, open-kneed breeches, buskin-like leg-flaps, two belts, basket, gun, and goatskin umbrella; long Mahometan-style moustaches.

Returned to the east-point hill and observed the current only ran close to shore on the ebb tide — realized the danger was avoidable with tide-timing; yet was too terrified to try retrieving the boat that way.
Resolved to build a second canoe so as to have one on each side of the island, rather than risk the east-point current again.
Found the print of a single naked human foot in the sand near the shore going toward the boat — stood thunderstruck, then fled home in terror, sleeping nothing that night.
After the footprint shock, concluded the print was most likely left by mainland savages blown to the island in their canoes — they had come and gone without staying.
The 'Call upon Me' scripture verse came to mind early one morning amid fear-filled thoughts about savages; rose cheerful and comforted — fear subsided enough to go out again.

Hid in the castle for three days and nights, reduced to barley-cakes and water, and nearly ruined his goats by not milking them — finally ventured out only when starvation and the goats' suffering forced him.
Returned to the shore and measured the footprint against his own foot — the print was considerably larger; confirmed it was not his; filled with vapours and shook like a man with ague.
In panic considered demolishing his enclosures, digging up his corn-fields, and tearing down the bower to erase all traces of habitation — then stepped back from these fear-driven schemes.

After a night of confusion, came to a calmer conclusion: the island is occasionally visited by straggling savages driven by wind, not settled by them; resolved to prepare a retreat rather than destroy his own work.

Built a second fortification: a new semicircular outer wall using the twelve-year-old double row of trees, thickened ten feet deep with earth, with seven holes fitted with all seven salvaged muskets as fixed cannon — took many months.

Planted approximately twenty thousand osier-like stakes between the outer wall and the surrounding ground — in two years a thick grove, in five or six a completely impassable wood hiding all trace of habitation.

Fenced a secret three-acre enclosure in the hidden interior woods and moved ten young she-goats and two he-goats there as a backup herd — took about a month to fence; spent two years under the anxiety of the footprint.
Thought he saw a boat far out at sea from the west hill — too far to be sure; resolved never to go out again without a perspective glass.

Reached the far west end of the island for the first time and found clear evidence of regular cannibal landings: skulls, bones, flesh, and the remains of a fire — understood he had been providentially cast on the savages' unused side.
Came down to the SW shore and discovered the cannibal feast site: ground strewn with skulls, hands, feet, and bones, with a fire pit and circular earthen cockpit — vomited from the horror and fled.
Spent almost two years confined to his three enclosures — castle, bower, and goat enclosure — firing his gun not once, and wearing two pistols with a cutlass on his belt whenever he went out.

Spent weeks planning an ambush attack on the cannibals — scouted firing positions on the hillside, loaded two muskets with slugs and smaller balls and the fowling-piece with swan-shot — but never executed the attack.

Abandoned the ambush plan after two to three months of fruitless morning watches — moral reasoning convinced him he had no right to attack the cannibals since they had done him no injury; thanked God on his knees for being kept from blood-guiltiness.
Moved the canoe from the west side of the island to a hidden cove on the east end, under high rocks in currents the savages would not dare enter — removed all trace of any human habitation.

Discovered a large natural cave in a great rock while cutting charcoal wood in the interior — entered to find a dying old he-goat inside; the cave went deeper to a vast inner vault of dry, gravel-floored rock that sparkled with minerals under candlelight.

Moved the magazine of powder (including ~60 lb recovered from a sea-wet barrel's dry core) and all spare arms to the new inner cave; kept only five cannon-mounted muskets and 2-3 lb of powder at the castle.

In December of the twenty-third year, saw a fire on his side of the island — spied through his glass nine naked savages sitting round it with two canoes; retreated to the castle, armed everything, and waited; savages left on the flood tide.

Went down to the shore after the savages departed and found blood, bones, and flesh — remnants of a cannibal feast; was filled with fresh indignation and renewed plans for murder, but they did not return for fifteen months.

On May 16 of the twenty-fourth year, during a storm with lightning and thunder, heard two cannon shots fired at sea — immediately lit a signal fire on the hilltop all night; by daybreak could see a faint shape far out to the east.
Discovered from the south rocks that the distant shape was a shipwreck on the concealed rocks — the same rocks that had saved him from the current; no survivors could be identified.
Found the corpse of a drowned boy washed ashore from the wreck — a seaman's waistcoat, linen drawers, a blue linen shirt, two pieces of eight, and a tobacco pipe; the pipe valued far above the money.

Provisioned the canoe (bread, water, rum, raisins, rice, barley cakes, milk, cheese, umbrella, compass) and launched toward the wreck; at the northeast point paused in fear of the currents — studied the flood tidal set from a hill and worked out a safe return route along the north shore.

Sailed to the Spanish wreck on the flood current — found two drowned men embracing, a starving dog, two chests, a cask of rum, powder-horn, fire-shovel, tongs, two brass kettles, and a copper pot; brought them back to the island in under two hours.

Opened the salvaged chests: found cordial waters in silver-tipped bottles, sweetmeats, shirts, linen handkerchiefs, neckcloths, about 1,100 pieces of eight in three bags, six gold doubloons and small gold bars weighing near a pound, and two pairs of shoes.

On a sleepless night in March of the twenty-fourth year, lay awake reviewing his whole life and comparing the serene early island years with the anxiety, fear, and care that had consumed him since discovering the footprint.

Dreamed of two canoes bringing eleven savages to shore to kill a prisoner — the prisoner escaped into the grove, knelt before him, became his servant, and in the dream he felt certain he could reach the mainland using the man as pilot.
Woke from the escape dream into sharp dejection; resolved to attempt to capture one of the savages' condemned prisoners if they came ashore again.
Spent more than a year and a half on daily watches at the west end and southwest corner of the island, scanning for canoes, but none appeared.
Five canoes with at least thirty savages landed on his side of the island — a cannibal feast; watched from the hilltop with his perspective glass as two prisoners were brought out for slaughter.
One condemned prisoner broke free and ran toward the grove; Crusoe descended, knocked down one pursuer with his gun-stock and shot the second dead — the first human blood he has shed on the island.

The rescued savage approached trembling, knelt every few steps, kissed the ground, and set Crusoe's foot upon his own head — an act of submission and pledge of lifelong service; the first man's voice Crusoe had heard in over twenty-five years.
The stunned pursuer revived; Crusoe lent Friday his sword, and Friday cut off the man's head at one blow; then buried both bodies in the sand before following Crusoe to the inner cave.
Gave the rescued man bread, raisins, and water at the cave; showed him a rice-straw pallet and blanket; the man lay down and slept.
Named the rescued man Friday, after the day of rescue; taught him to say 'Master', 'Yes', and 'No'; gave him milk and bread at the cave that night.

Marched with Friday back to the cannibal feast site — blood, bones, skulls, mangled flesh; Friday signed that four prisoners had been brought, three eaten, and he was the fourth; had Friday burn all remains in a heap.

Made Friday a linen drawers, goatskin jerkin, and hare-skin cap — Friday's first clothing; lodged him in a small tent between the two fortifications, with a barred door to the inner cave for security.

Took Friday hunting; shot a kid — Friday thought the gun was aimed at him and knelt begging for his life; then watched in astonishment as a parrot was shot dead at distance; would not touch the gun for days after, speaking to it when alone to beg it not to kill him.
Fed Friday boiled and roasted kid; after tasting roast meat Friday declared he would never eat man's flesh again.
Taught Friday to beat and sift corn and bake bread; enlarged the crop field to feed two mouths; Friday worked willingly and hard.
The year after Friday's arrival became the pleasantest year of island life — Friday learned to talk well, Crusoe had use for his tongue again, and he began genuinely to love Friday.
Asked Friday whether his nation conquered in battle — begun the first extended English conversation; Friday said his nation generally won but he was taken when outnumbered in one place.
Friday confirmed his nation also eats captives; revealed he had himself been on the island before on a cannibal feast — a party that ate twenty men, two women, and one child on the northwest shore.
Friday described the sea route from the island to the mainland — always a current one way in the morning, the other in the afternoon; said he could be reached in two canoes (meaning one large boat).
Began instructing Friday in the Christian faith — the true God, Christ, prayer; Friday responded eagerly and compared God favourably to Benamuckee.

Friday posed the unanswerable question: if God is stronger than the devil, why does God not kill the devil now? Crusoe was stumped, fell back on God reserving judgment, and Friday drew the corollary: so God preserves all — wicked men, the devil — to repent and be pardoned.
Prayed for ability to instruct Friday savingly; then delivered a long discourse on redemption, repentance, and Christ — and found the instruction deepened his own faith as much as Friday's.
Taught Friday to shoot; gave him a knife and made him a belt with a hatchet in a frog; told him the history of the island, the wreck, and England.

Friday identified a ruined boat on shore as similar to one that came to his country — then said his nation saved seventeen white men from drowning, and those men were still living among his people after about four years.
From the hilltop Friday saw his homeland across the water, jumped and danced with joy, crying 'there my nation' — his longing for home was unmistakable.

Became jealous and suspicious that Friday might betray him to his nation; pulled back in warmth and familiarity for several weeks — then recognised he had wronged the honest creature and was sorry for it.
Crusoe probed Friday daily during the jealousy period but found every answer honest and innocent — suspicion dissolved entirely on its own.
Crusoe and Friday walked up the hill together and Crusoe asked whether Friday wished to return to his nation — Friday said yes but only if Crusoe came too.
Friday refused to take the canoe home alone, offering Crusoe the hatchet and saying 'you take kill Friday' rather than be sent away — tears in his eyes.
Crusoe resolved to build a large canoe and attempt a crossing to the mainland to join the seventeen bearded men Friday had described.
Crusoe and Friday felled a large fustic-like tree and spent about a month hewing and shaping a large periagua capable of carrying twenty men, then another fortnight rolling her into the water.
Crusoe fitted the new large canoe with a cedar mast and a makeshift shoulder-of-mutton sail sewn from two surviving pieces of old sails, plus an anchor and cable.
Spent nearly two months rigging the large canoe — fitted a foresail, stay, and a working rudder; taught Friday sailing and rudder management until he became an expert sailor.
Reached the twenty-seventh year on the island; kept the anniversary with thanksgiving, having a strong impression his deliverance was at hand — expected not to be there another year.
Stored the new canoe in a purpose-built dock in the creek during the rainy season — hauled up at high-water mark, dammed at low tide, thatched with boughs; planned to launch in November or December.

Friday spotted three canoes of savages approaching while searching for turtles — twenty-one savages, three prisoners, three canoes; Crusoe and Friday armed fully and marched toward them through the wood.
During the march Crusoe's fury abated — he reasoned he had no right to attack savages who had done him no wrong and were innocent as to him; resolved to observe only and act as God should direct.
Crusoe and Friday opened fire on the savages from the tree line — first volley killed 3 and wounded several; second volley with swan-shot killed 2 more and wounded many; Friday outshot Crusoe.

Crusoe rushed out of the wood, cut the bound European prisoner free — found him a Spaniard; gave him rum and bread, then a pistol and sword; the Spaniard fought his captors furiously despite his weakness.

Friday pursued fleeing savages with his hatchet and killed most; the Spaniard took a fowling-piece and pursued two more; four savages escaped into the sea and canoe — total body count: 17 killed, 4 escaped.
The rescued prisoner identified himself as Spanish and one of the seventeen white bearded men who had been living peaceably among the Caribs — confirming Crusoe's surmise.
Found Friday's father bound in the savages' canoe — cut him free; Friday's reunion with him was explosive with grief and joy, the most affecting scene Crusoe had ever witnessed.
Friday sprinted home and back in under a quarter hour to fetch water and bread for his father — water revived him more than all the rum.
Friday carried the Spaniard on his back to the canoe, paddled both men to the creek, then fetched the second canoe — all with extraordinary swiftness and care.
Crusoe and Friday built a tent of old sails and boughs outside the outer fence, set up rice-straw beds with blankets for Friday's father and the Spaniard.
Crusoe reflected that his island was now a three-subject kingdom: Friday (Protestant), Friday's father (Pagan/cannibal), Spaniard (Papist) — he allowed liberty of conscience throughout.
Friday buried the savage dead and erased all trace of the feast site; Friday was interpreter between Crusoe, the Spaniard, and Friday's father.

Friday's father reported the four escaped savages likely drowned or driven ashore to hostile coasts; if they survived, they would have told their people the attackers were heavenly spirits — fire from the gods — and so the island was never attempted again.

Crusoe held a serious discourse with the Spaniard: sixteen Europeans (Spanish and five Portuguese) are living among the Caribs on the mainland — from a Rio de la Plata ship, no arms, no powder, near starved, hoping for escape.

Crusoe offered to relieve the sixteen Europeans but expressed fear of treachery — dreaded being delivered to the Inquisition in New Spain; the Spaniard gave a solemn oath of allegiance, pledging to take Crusoe's side to the last drop of his blood.

The Spaniard prudently advised deferring rescue for at least half a year — current food stores are insufficient for twenty and for victualling a vessel; Crusoe agreed to wait another harvest; the Spaniard, Friday's father, and Friday to help cultivate more land.
All four inhabitants dug and planted expanded fields — 22 bushels of barley and 16 jars of rice sown (all seed reserves used); then cleared timber for about a dozen large planks for a vessel.
Harvest yielded above 220 bushels of barley and proportionate rice — enough to provision all sixteen Spaniards and victualling a ship for any American voyage.
Boosted the goat herd by about twenty young kids (shooting dams and saving kids on rotating hunting turns); cured a massive raisin harvest — enough to fill 60-80 barrels.

In October, Crusoe dispatched the Spaniard and Friday's father to the mainland with a musket each, 8 charges of powder and ball, and provisions for about 8 days — to fetch the sixteen Europeans under sworn contract.

Eight days after the departure, an English ship (with an English long-boat) appeared at anchor about two and a half leagues away — 11 men landed, 3 of them prisoners; Crusoe stayed hidden on secret providential hints that English ships had no good business here.
Crusoe revealed himself to the three marooned prisoners — the English captain, his mate, and a passenger — speaking first in Spanish then English, and offered to help them.
The English captain identified himself as commander of the ship, whose crew had mutinied, barely spared his life, and set him ashore on the island with his mate and a passenger.

Crusoe negotiated a sworn pact with the captain: while on the island the captain would obey Crusoe's orders and surrender arms on demand; in return Crusoe would help recover the ship, and the captain would carry Crusoe and Friday to England free.

The first shore party of mutineers was attacked: two ringleaders killed or clubbed down, remaining three bound and taken prisoner after swearing loyalty; first boat secured, oars and sails removed, and hole staved in her bottom.
Three more straggling mutineers heard the guns and surrendered to the captain; the island-side victory was complete with all first-party mutineers killed, wounded, or captured.

Crusoe told the captain his whole twenty-seven-year island history; the captain wept and could not speak, believing Crusoe had been preserved on purpose to save his life; the captain admired the fortress and hidden grove.
Crusoe and the captain staved the first longboat to prevent the ship's remaining crew from reclaiming it; salvaged brandy, rum, biscuit, powder, and sugar from her.
The ship fired signals for the boat; getting no response, she hoisted a second boat with ten armed men and rowed toward shore — Crusoe and the captain prepared to receive them.
Prisoners separated: two untrusted men sent with Friday to the inner cave, bound and provisioned; two more taken into service on captain's recommendation; force grew to seven well-armed men.

Second shore party (ten men) found the first longboat staved and stripped; fired volleys to signal companions, got no answer, and briefly went back to the ship — then returned to shore leaving three men guarding the second boat at anchor.

Seven men from the second party came ashore to search; three stayed in the boat at anchor — making the boat impossible to seize directly; they searched and shouted but found nothing, then resolved to return to the ship.

Crusoe devised a hallooing stratagem: sent Friday and the captain's mate to lure the seamen westward with shouts; the seven men crossed the creek after the voice, leaving only two men in the second boat.

Crusoe's party surprised and seized the two men left in the second boat; one easily defected to Crusoe's side; Friday and the captain's mate kept drawing the seven-man search party deep into the woods until dark.
At nightfall the exhausted seven-man party returned to the creek; Crusoe drew the ambuscade closer; the boatswain (principal ringleader) and one companion were shot, a third fled.
Crusoe used a parley stratagem: a defected crewman called Tom Smith by name, claiming fifty men and the captain — all remaining mutineers laid down arms and surrendered.

Crusoe kept himself hidden as 'the governor'; the captain maintained the fiction of fifty men and an English commander of the island — Will Atkins (first to lay hands on the captain) singled out for pretended execution to terrify the rest.

Prisoners divided: Atkins and two worst sent pinioned to the inner cave; others held at the bower; Crusoe's plan was to enlist five of them to help retake the ship, holding the remaining five as hostages whose lives would be forfeit if the five were unfaithful.

Twelve men went aboard at midnight; the captain and mate knocked down the second mate and carpenter and secured the main deck; the other boat secured the forecastle; the new rebel captain was shot through the head in the round-house — ship taken without further deaths.

Seven-gun signal fired from the recovered ship; Crusoe heard it from shore, slept, then was woken to the captain calling him 'Governor' — the ship lay at anchor half a mile off, and Crusoe was so overcome he could not speak.

The captain brought Crusoe a full supply of provisions and clothing — six shirts, suit, gloves, shoes, hat, stockings, wine, tobacco, beef, pork, biscuit, sugar, flour, lemons; Crusoe found the European clothes awkward after twenty-seven years in goatskin.

Crusoe, dressed in new clothes as governor, confronted the five remaining prisoners — told them Providence had ensnared them and he had authority to execute them as pirates; then maneuvered the two worst into asking to be left on the island rather than taken to England.

Two of the five men who had chosen to stay on the island swam to the ship next morning begging to be taken on board, fearing murder from the other three; after promises of amendment they were taken on board and later whipped.

Left the island 19 December 1686 after twenty-eight years, two months, and nineteen days — took the goatskin cap, umbrella, a parrot, and both stores of coin; delivered from this second captivity on the same day of the month as his escape from the Moors.

Arrived in England 11 June 1687 — thirty-five years absent; found himself a complete stranger; father dead, mother and family all extinct except two sisters and two nephews; no provision had been made for him as he had been given over for dead.
Ship owners rewarded Crusoe with almost £200 sterling on the captain's account of how he saved ship and men.
Sailed to Lisbon with Friday to inquire about his Brazil plantation; found the Portuguese captain (his old rescuer), now elderly and retired from the sea.

Portuguese captain reported the plantation partner was still alive and rich; Crusoe's share had been administered by trustees, then appropriated — one-third to the king, two-thirds to the Monastery of St Augustine — but would be restored on his claiming it; trustees' sons held twelve years of accumulated produce.

Portuguese captain revealed he had received six to eight years of plantation profits on Crusoe's behalf — about 470 moidores of gold owed, partly spent on his own losses after being shipwrecked en route to Lisbon; gave Crusoe 160 moidores cash and deeds to a ship share as security.

Crusoe took 100 of the 160 moidores, returned the rest, gave the captain a receipt, and released him from the debt of 470 moidores — rewarding the captain with a 100-moidores-per-year annuity for life and 50 moidores per year to his son after him.
Crusoe registered his name and an affidavit of being alive with a Lisbon notary on the Portuguese captain's advice, then sent a procuration to a merchant in Brazil to secure the plantation claim.

Within seven months a large packet arrived from Brazil: 1,174 moidores balance from first six years, 3,240 moidores from the next four years, 872 moidores acknowledged by the Prior of St Augustine, 1,200 chests of sugar, 800 rolls of tobacco, and the rest in gold — total wealth suddenly above £5,000 sterling with an estate worth over £1,000 per year.
Crusoe turned pale and grew sick on receiving all his goods and wealth at once — so overwhelmed by sudden joy that a physician was called and he was let blood to relieve the shock.
Sent 100 pounds to the captain's widow in London via a Lisbon merchant, promising further supply if he lived.
Sent 100 pounds each to his two sisters in England, one a widow, one in an unhappy marriage.

Wrote letters of thanks to the Prior of St Augustine, the two trustees, and his Brazil partner; directed 500 moidores to the monastery and 372 to the poor; sent silk and cloth gifts to the partner's wife and daughters; gave the partner power to manage the plantation and send profits to the Portuguese captain.
Sold his Lisbon cargo and converted all effects into bills of exchange in preparation for return to England.

Resolved to travel overland to England rather than by sea — two ships he had selected were lost (one taken by Algerines, one wrecked near Torbay); set out from Lisbon with a company of six travelers and five servants, Friday included.
Company reached Pamplona and found the Pyrenees snowbound — cold was insufferable to Crusoe after decades in a tropical climate.
Company stranded at Pamplona for twenty days by impassable snow — the severest winter in living European memory; Friday frightened by his first sight of snow and cold.
Set out from Pamplona with a local guide on 15 November, taking a southerly detour to approach the Pyrenees from a lower angle; crossed the mountains by winding ways and descended into Gascony.
Three wolves and a bear attacked the party's guide in the Gascony forest; Friday rode up boldly and shot the wolf at close range, saving the wounded guide.

Friday deliberately provoked a huge bear by throwing a stone at its head, then ran it on a chase toward a large oak tree in the Gascony forest, to the astonishment and growing amusement of the company.
Friday led the bear on a mock hunt up a tree branch, dancing it to the edge, then slid down and shot it dead through the ear — a deliberate display of forest craft that amused the whole company.

On the plain near the village in Gascony the company encountered a pack of about a hundred wolves advancing in formation; fired a volley that killed four and wounded several; routed them with shouting and a second volley into their rear.

Three separate wolf troops surrounded the company as night fell — they pushed through at a hard trot; on approaching the wood pass saw a riderless saddled horse flee with sixteen or seventeen wolves behind it.

A second, fiercer wolf attack at a wood entrance — bodies of two men and a horse already devoured; party made a defensive triangle behind a fallen log and fought off roughly three hundred wolves; killed about sixty in all using volleys, a gunpowder train on the timber, and sword-work on the lamed survivors.
Party reached Toulouse safely; locals told them they were lucky to survive — the horses drew the wolves and standing still was the near-fatal error.
Arrived at Dover on 14 January after travelling through France from Toulouse to Paris to Calais — bills of exchange paid, estate secured.

Sold the Brazil plantation to the merchant-trustees for 32,800 pieces of eight (33,000 promised; 200 retained for the Portuguese captain's annuity) — the first part of a life of Providence's chequered work concluded.
The captain's widow became Crusoe's principal guide and privy-counsellor in England; fully trusted with the security of his effects; her integrity absolute throughout.
Widow dissuaded Crusoe from going abroad for almost seven years; during that time he took in his two nephews — bred the elder as a gentleman, placed the younger to sea under a captain.
Married — advantageously and without dissatisfaction — and had three children: two sons and one daughter.
Wife died; nephew returned from a successful voyage to Spain; Crusoe agreed to sail with him as a private trader to the East Indies — departure in 1694.

In 1694 voyaged to his island-colony on the East Indies run: found the Spaniards and English mutineers there; heard their history of conflict, cooperation, and Caribbean battles; stayed about twenty days and left supplies — arms, powder, clothes, tools, and two English workmen (a carpenter and a smith).
Divided the island lands among the settlers, reserving overall property to himself; formally engaged them not to leave.
From Brazil sent a bark with more people, seven women (for service or as wives), five cows, sheep, and hogs to the island colony.

communication.label: Communication style
communication.line: How they like to be spoken to.

life.label: Life
life.line: Robinson Crusoe (born York 1632, anglicised from Kreutznaer); compulsive wanderer — Brazil four years, wrecked 1659, sole survivor; twenty-eight years on the Island of Despair ended 19 December 1686; returned England January 1688 with sudden great wealth; married, had three children, wife died; sailed again in 1694 — the wandering life resumed.

life/island.label: Island survival
life/island.line: Robinson Crusoe on the Island of Despair (9°22'N, Orinoco) from 30 September 1659 to 19 December 1686 — twenty-eight years; sole survivor, fortress built, farm running, four companions at peak; island felt as beloved home; mutiny resolved, deliverance overwhelming; revisited in 1694 on the East Indies voyage, found the colony thriving, divided the land and sent livestock — still the island's nominal proprietor.

life/island/animals.label: Island animals and domestics
life/island/animals.line: Island household fully matured: ship's dog (sixteen faithful years, died of old age), Poll the parrot (twenty-six years, best of all parrots), two tame cats from wild descendants, and a goat herd of 43 animals in five pastures with a dairy — food security complete; a second secret herd kept as backup; all the original animals eventually dead or replaced.

life/island/camp.label: Island camp and fortification
life/island/camp.line: A layered, invisible fortress-home: cave-apartment (warehouse, kitchen, cellar) behind a palisade grown into trees, a second ten-foot earth wall with seven musket-cannon on mounts, then twenty thousand osier stakes as impenetrable wood — backed by a vast natural inner cave for the ammunition magazine; Friday now lodged in the inter-wall space with a barred inner door; the castle is home in the deepest sense.

life/island/daily-life.label: Island daily life and food
life/island/daily-life.line: Daily life fully established in the eleventh year and beyond: firm routine (scripture thrice, gun walk, food prep), post-calendar with Sabbath marks, full goatskin outfit (jacket, open-kneed breeches, leg-flaps, belts, pouches, umbrella, Turkish whiskers), bread from his own crop, and a working dairy — food supply is abundant; only society is lacking.

life/island/escape.label: Escape plans and boats
life/island/escape.line: Twenty-seven years of escape striving resolved: two unlaunched canoes, one swept-out scare, a circumnavigation, the large fitted periagua, sixteen Spaniards planned — then superseded by the English ship's mutiny; the ship is now recovered and lies at anchor, Crusoe's deliverance finally and visibly in hand.

life/island/escape/boats.label: Boat-building and physical escape attempts
life/island/escape/boats.line: Twenty years of boat frustration — first ship's boat unmovable, giant cedar canoe stranded and rotted, a second smaller canoe dug half a mile to water, swept to sea on circumnavigation; now a large fitted periagua sits in a creek dock, the first vessel capable of the forty-mile mainland crossing.

life/island/escape/mainland-plan.label: Continental escape plan
life/island/escape/mainland-plan.line: The continental plan: Friday revealed sixteen Spaniards and Portuguese living among Caribs forty miles away — Crusoe plans to cross with the large periagua, but fears Inquisition treachery and deferred rescue one harvest on the Spaniard's prudent advice to build food first.

life/island/farming.label: Island farming and crops
life/island/farming.line: Farming arc complete: from first miraculous barley sprout to a 220-bushel harvest sufficient to provision twenty people and victual a vessel — barley and rice, one annual sowing for ~40 bushels baseline; field enlarged each time the party grew; wild fruit, grapes-as-raisins, and goat dairy round out the food supply.

life/island/geography.label: Island geography and location
life/island/geography.line: Uninhabited island at 9°22'N (Island of Despair) in the mouth of the Orinoco; the land to the west-northwest is Trinidad; Caribs use the northwest and west shores as regular cannibal feast grounds — Crusoe's camp is providentially on the east/north, their unused side; Spaniards lie somewhere to the west.

life/island/geography/cannibal-shore.label: Cannibal shore and savage presence
life/island/geography/cannibal-shore.line: The west and southwest shores are the Caribs' regular feast ground — skulls, bones, flesh, fire pits, and earthen cockpit found there; Crusoe's camp is on the east/north, their unused side; the Spaniards lie somewhere further west, their cruelties remembered by all Carib nations.

life/island/geography/physical.label: Island physical geography
life/island/geography/physical.line: Island at 9°22'N in the Orinoco gulf — high central hill, northward ridge, two small islands three leagues west; interior tidal creek, savannahs, and garden valley; east hazard of a rock ledge two leagues out; Orinoco tidal currents; land to the northwest confirmed as Trinidad; struck by a major earthquake in year three.

life/island/milestones.label: Island time milestones
life/island/milestones.line: Twenty-eight years marked by solemn anniversaries and date-coincidences — fourth year's resignation, year fifteen's footprint, years twenty-five to twenty-seven with Friday as a different kind of life altogether; the three years with Friday the happiest; Crusoe tracks his island captivity as a distinct chain of providential chapters, now closed.

life/island/mutiny.label: Mutiny and ship recovery
life/island/mutiny.line: The English ship mutiny resolved: captain marooned with mate and passenger, pact sworn with Crusoe; shore campaign defeated both landing parties; ship retaken at midnight — rebel captain shot dead, seven guns fired as signal; two worst prisoners maneuvered into volunteering to stay on the island.

life/island/mutiny/shore-campaign.label: Shore campaign against mutineers
life/island/mutiny/shore-campaign.line: A two-stage shore campaign: first party ambushed and ringleaders killed; second party of ten lured into the woods by hallooing stratagem, second boat seized; all surrendered after a parley fiction of fifty men; boatswain (chief ringleader) killed in the night ambush.

life/island/religion.label: Island religious awakening
life/island/religion.line: Faith cracked open by island fever has matured through grief, fear, and scruple into a disciplined daily practice — firm thanksgiving, Sabbath observance, a rule to obey secret providential hints, and a standing moral refusal to attack innocent-as-to-him cannibals; religious calm can still be overwhelmed by desperate longing, but the underlying anchor is deep.

life/island/religion/awakening.label: Religious awakening (fever and early faith)
life/island/religion/awakening.line: The June fever — delirium dream, first crying prayer, first grace, natural-theology reflection by the sea, and the Bible verse 'I will deliver thee' — cracked open a dormant conscience and set a daily scripture habit in motion.

life/island/religion/moral-reasoning.label: Moral and providential reasoning
life/island/religion/moral-reasoning.line: Cannibals are innocent-as-to-him — a firm standing refusal to act as executioner without a clear call; but that scruple dissolved at once when a bound Christian prisoner appeared at the feast; Providence mercifully screens men from dangers, and Crusoe's own defiance of Providence is his named original sin.

life/island/religion/settled-faith.label: Settled faith and daily practice
life/island/religion/settled-faith.line: Through grief, anguish, and self-condemnation, faith settled into a firm daily rhythm — Scripture, Sabbath, thanksgiving, secret providential hints; teaching Friday deepened Crusoe's own faith and turned island captivity into gratitude; three years of instruction brought both to full Christian peace.

life/island/savages.label: Savage and cannibal encounters
life/island/savages.line: Twenty-seven years of uneasy coexistence with mainland Caribs — from paralysing footprint terror and two years confined, to deliberate moral restraint, to a battle that killed 17 of 21 savages and freed both a Spaniard and Friday's father; the four who escaped in the canoe likely died in the gale.

life/island/savages/early-presence.label: Early savage presence and fear
life/island/savages/early-presence.line: From the footprint in year fifteen to fifteen years of concealment, tidal-pattern observation, and moral restraint — a terror that shaped nearly all of Crusoe's outdoor life but never led to an attack.

life/island/savages/rescues.label: Rescues and the battle
life/island/savages/rescues.line: Plan to seize a prisoner pilot was fulfilled when Friday ran to Crusoe; the follow-up battle killed 17 of 21 savages and freed both a Spaniard and Friday's father — four escapees likely lost at sea in the gale.

life/island/stores.label: Island stores and supplies
life/island/stores.line: Two salvages complete — original wreck (11 trips: arms, tools, food, books, instruments, coin) and Spanish wreck (~1,100 pieces of eight, gold, cordial waters, kettles, powder); all craft needs improvised; powder low (~60 lb dry, one barrel); coin worthless; bread fully operational.

life/island/stores/craft.label: Island improvised craft and tools
life/island/stores/craft.line: All craft needs improvised over the years: pottery (kiln, wheel, glazed pots), mortar and pestle, sieves, oven, wicker baskets, clay pipe, goat-tallow candles — self-sufficient in every household tool.

life/island/stores/weapons.label: Island arms and powder
life/island/stores/weapons.line: Castle keeps five muskets mounted; all spare arms (2 fowling-pieces, 3 muskets) and the powder magazine (~60 lb dry) moved to the inner cave — powder dangerously low, within one barrel.

life/origins.label: Origins and early voyages
life/origins.line: Born 1632 York (Robinson Kreutznaer, anglicised to Crusoe); third son; left home at 18 against father's counsel; first ship foundered at Yarmouth Roads 1651; one profitable Guinea voyage; then enslaved by Moors at Sallee and escaped with Xury.

life/return-england.label: Return to England
life/return-england.line: Returned England January 1688 after thirty-five years — family nearly extinct, two sisters helped; resolved overland route after two ships miscarried; widowed on arrival, found sudden great wealth; seven years settled before the wandering life resumed in 1694.

money.label: Money
money.line: Fortune ran from modest Guinea profit (£300) and Brazil plantation start to sudden great wealth — £5,000 sterling cash and a Brazil estate sold for 32,800 pieces of eight; first acts of that wealth were repaying every benefactor and settling annuities; the captain's widow held his money through it all.

money-style.label: Money style
money-style.line: How they handle money: discipline, risk, planning.

people.label: People
people.line: Parents warned against the sea; Xury sold — a standing regret; the Guinea captain died and removed his best counsel; the Portuguese captain a lifelong trusted benefactor; family nearly extinct on return — two sisters found and helped; Wells the one friendly neighbour in Brazil.

people/captain-widow.label: Captain's widow (steward)
people/captain-widow.line: Faithful steward and privy-counsellor throughout — held his money thirty-five years in trust, was relieved with £100 on his return, and kept his effects and person stable in England for seven years; her integrity was absolute and his trust in her complete.

people/english-captain.label: English ship's captain
people/english-captain.line: Commander of the English ship, mutinied against and marooned with his mate and a passenger — allied to Crusoe by sworn pact; deliverance is a standing hope between them.

people/father.label: Father
people/father.line: Wise, grave merchant from Bremen; pleaded earnestly against the sea — his prophetic counsel is a standing weight on Crusoe's conscience, declared fulfilled aloud in the fever's worst hour.

people/friday.label: Friday
people/friday.line: Crusoe's devoted companion — faithful, loving, fearless in battle, and now bound for England with him; jealousy dissolved when he proved wholly trustworthy; his filial joy at his father's rescue was the most affecting scene Crusoe ever witnessed.

people/friday-father.label: Friday's father
people/friday-father.line: Friday's father — found bound in the savages' canoe, near dead; Friday's reunion with him was one of the most affecting things Crusoe ever witnessed; a pagan and former cannibal, now a guest on the island.

people/friday/character.label: Friday's character, appearance, and habits
people/friday/character.line: About twenty-six, tall and well-made with a sweet smiling face; voluntarily renounced cannibalism; repugnant to salt; cool and deadly under fire; expert sailor; awed by the gun at first; had never seen a metal sword yet cut off a head at a blow.

people/friday/faith.label: Friday's faith and teaching
people/friday/faith.line: Crusoe opened Friday's mind to Scripture and Christ; Friday's probing questions — especially why God does not kill the devil — deepened Crusoe's own faith more than private reading ever had; Friday reached the conclusion that God preserves all to repent and be pardoned; Crusoe also identified his people's priestcraft.

people/guinea-captain.label: Guinea captain (first)
people/guinea-captain.line: Honest, plain-dealing captain who befriended Crusoe on the Guinea voyage; taught him navigation and acted with disinterested honesty — his death left Crusoe without his most trusted guide, a loss that set ruin in motion.

people/mother.label: Mother
people/mother.line: York woman of the Robinson family; refused to intercede for the sea voyage — both parents stood against him.

people/portuguese-captain.label: Portuguese captain (rescue)
people/portuguese-captain.line: Generous rescuer and lifelong honest steward — received plantation profits on Crusoe's behalf, repaid what he could despite own shipwreck losses, and was rewarded with an annuity as Crusoe's first act of restored wealth; deep gratitude and full trust sustained across thirty-five years.

people/spaniard.label: The rescued Spaniard
people/spaniard.line: Rescued European — Spanish, brave and candid; swore personal allegiance to Crusoe and brokered the plan to bring sixteen stranded countrymen across; prudently advised waiting a harvest before attempting the rescue.

people/wells.label: Wells (Brazil neighbour)
people/wells.line: Portuguese-born of English parents; plantation neighbour in Brazil — sociable partner in early planting years, the one human connection in an otherwise solitary existence.

people/xury.label: Xury
people/xury.line: Boy slave and escape companion; swore faithfulness, proved cheerful and selfless — sold to the Portuguese captain with a freedom bond; parting is a standing regret.

temperament.label: Temperament
temperament.line: Compulsive wanderer who defies counsel and settles to nothing — names restlessness his original sin; practical and resourceful under mortal danger; conscience cracked open by island fever and now in earnest daily faith; repays loyalty generously; solitude felt as embodied privation; wary that gratitude rarely survives advantage.

temperament/practical.label: Practical and resourceful character
temperament/practical.line: Patient, relentless improviser who exhausts every option — forty-two days for a single shelf board, months to crack pottery, years to perfect bread; approaches strangers cautiously; plans systematically but plunges into big projects before counting the full cost; keeps presence of mind under mortal danger.

temperament/religion.label: Religious and moral character
temperament/religion.line: Conscience long suppressed by seafaring company and cracked open only by island fever — never thanked God through Sallee, rescue, or Brazil; now in settled daily gratitude and resignation to Providence after working through fever, anguish, and self-condemnation; teaching Friday deepened his own faith; escape impulse can still override calm, but the anchor is firm.

temperament/wandering.label: Wandering and restlessness
temperament/wandering.line: Has a deep, unkillable drive to wander — names it his original sin (could have been worth 100,000 moidores had he stayed in Brazil); great wealth, marriage, and seven years of a widow's counsel could not hold him; blames his own obstinacy in hindsight yet sailed again in 1694.

work/brazil-plantation.label: Brazil plantation
work/brazil-plantation.line: Tobacco and sugar plantation at All Saints' Bay, Brazil — grew prosperously over four years, abandoned to wanderlust in 1659; thirty-five-year claim recovered in full on return (1,174 + 3,240 + 872 moidores in accumulated produce); plantation sold to the trustees for 32,800 pieces of eight and the estate closed out.

all-mutineers-surrendered.text: All remaining mutineers surrendered and begged for their lives after the parley stratagem; they were all bound, and the second boat seized.

ambush-plan-prepared.text: Abandoned the ambush plan entirely — concluded through moral reasoning he had no right to attack the cannibals who had done him no injury; resolved to conceal himself rather than attack unless directly threatened.

history.value: Planned and prepared an ambush at the cannibal fire site — loaded two muskets with slugs and the fowling-piece with swan-shot, scouted a concealed hillside position — but did not execute it.

arms-powder-in-cave.text: Transferred all spare arms (2 fowling-pieces, 3 muskets) and the powder magazine to the inner cave; keeps only five muskets mounted at the castle and 2-3 lb of powder there.

arrival-brazil.text: Arrived in Brazil at the Bay of All Saints (Bay de Todos los Santos) about twenty-two days after rescue.

arrival-england-1687.text: Arrived at Dover on 14 January — overland journey from Lisbon via Madrid, Pamplona, the Pyrenees, Toulouse, Paris, and Calais completed.

history.value: Arrived in England on 11 June 1687 — thirty-five years absent; found himself a complete stranger.
