barley-sprouted.text: The barley grew from a salvaged chicken-feed bag shaken out by the fortification — not miraculous, but still remarkable that any grains survived the rats and fell in ideal shade.

history.value: Barley and other grain husks shaken from a salvaged bag grew into ten or twelve green barley stalks — initially appeared miraculous; believed to be European barley.

basket-making.text: Made wicker baskets from living-stake twigs using basket-making knowledge absorbed as a boy watching craftsmen in York; now a reliable supply for carrying and storing.

bible-reading-begun.text: Began reading the New Testament every morning and evening from 4 July — first serious and regular scripture reading of his life.

bible-verse-deliverance.text: First Bible verse encountered by chance: 'Call on Me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver thee' — pondered often; deliverance seemed impossible yet the words held.

bible-verse-forsake.text: Opened the Bible to 'I will never, never leave thee, nor forsake thee' on a sad morning and felt the words addressed to him personally; concluded God's favour outweighs all worldly loss.

boat-abandoned-north-shore.text: Left the canoe in a safe harbour on the north shore — too afraid of the east-point current to bring it back; resigned to being without a boat on his home side of the island.

boatswain-killed.text: The boatswain — identified as the chief ringleader of the mutiny — was killed on the spot in the night ambush; a second man mortally wounded, a third fled.

brazil-cargo-proceeds.text: Total proceeds from cargo sold to the Portuguese captain (boat £80, leopard skin 20 ducats, lion skin 40 ducats, other goods) came to about 220 pieces of eight.

brazil-plantation-alive.text: Sold the Brazil plantation to the merchant-trustees for 32,800 pieces of eight net (the Portuguese captain's annuity charge retained); the estate is fully disposed of.

history.value: Brazil plantation partner is alive and grown very rich; Crusoe's share was appropriated — one-third to the king, two-thirds to the Monastery of St Augustine — but can be fully restored on his appearing; trustees' sons hold twelve years of accumulated produce for his account.

brazil-scruple-religion.text: Considered settling in Brazil but felt a growing scruple about having professed himself a Catholic there — regretted it when thinking of living and dying among them, though religion was not the main reason he chose England.

bread-gap-identified.text: Has now baked barley loaves and rice cakes — the full bread-production chain (mortar/pestle, sieves, oven) is operational; bread supply no longer a future aspiration but a present reality.

history.value: Bread stores so low that Crusoe reduced himself to one biscuit cake per day.
Identified the full chain of missing implements for bread: no plough, no harrow, no scythe, no mill, no sieves, no yeast, no salt, no oven — each must be improvised before the grain can be eaten.

calendar-post.text: Keeps time with a post-calendar: daily notches with weekly and monthly longer marks — only way to track days without books or pen.

camp-as-home.text: The discomfort of wandering a month without a fixed dwelling confirmed the camp as a true psychological home; resolved never again to go far from it.

camp-attachment.text: Strongly attached to the settled security of his camp — absence makes even a crude hutch feel like a perfect home

nudges.note: After a month wandering without fixed abode he felt the hutch as a perfect settlement; resolved never to go far again.

candles-made.text: Makes good candles from goat tallow with improvised wicks (rags, rope-yarn, or dried weed rind) — supplies light inside the cave.

cannibal-landing-site-found.text: Found clear evidence of regular cannibal landings on the west end of the island: skulls, bones, flesh, fire remains — the savages use this shore regularly; Crusoe's east/north camp is on the unused side.

cannibal-moral-reasoning.text: Reasoned that the cannibals commit their acts without consciousness of crime — comparing to how Christians put prisoners to the sword — and concluded they are innocent as to him; likened attacking them to the Spanish massacres in America.

cannibal-site-discovered.text: The SW shore was strewn with skulls, hands, feet, and other human bones, with a fire pit and a circular earthen cockpit — physical evidence of cannibal feasts on the island.

canoe-docked-for-rainy-season.text: The large canoe was secured in a tidal dock in the creek through the rainy season — thatched with boughs; Crusoe planned the mainland crossing for November/December.

canoe-fitted.text: Fitted the small canoe with a mast, sail (from salvaged ship's canvas), dry-storage lockers at each end, and a covered gun-slot — ready for coastal cruising.

canoe-hidden-east.text: Moved the canoe to a small hidden cove under high rocks on the east end of the island — in strong currents the savages would not enter; removed the mast, sail, and improvised anchor to leave no trace.

canoe-unlaunchable.text: Built a second, smaller canoe and dug a canal nearly half a mile to float it to the creek — near two years' work; first launched canoe he has had on the island.

history.value: The cedar canoe could not be moved to the water — tried digging a slope and planning a canal, but the canal alone would have taken ten to twelve years; abandoned with great reluctance and self-reproach for not counting the cost first.

captain-identity.text: The English captain was commander of the ship; his crew mutinied, barely spared his life, and marooned him with his mate and a passenger on the island.

captain-pact-terms.text: Captain swore that he and the ship (if recovered) would be wholly directed by Crusoe; in return Crusoe promised to help recover the ship and demanded free passage to England for himself and Friday.

captain-widow-relief.text: The captain's widow became Crusoe's principal adviser and trustee in England — fully trusted with all his effects; her unspotted integrity held throughout.

history.value: Sent the captain's widow 100 pounds from Lisbon and promised a further supply — her faithful stewardship over thirty-five years finally repaid.

captive-savage-plan.text: Resolved to capture one of the savages' condemned prisoners if a cannibal feast came ashore again — to use the captive as a pilot to the mainland; settled to watch and wait for the opportunity.

castle-name-adopted.text: Castle now has a double outer wall: a new semicircular wall using the grown twelve-year-old stakes, thickened ten feet with earth, seven musket-holes with all seven ship's muskets mounted in frames as fixed cannon — entry only via two removable ladders over the rock.

history.value: From the moment of the footprint scare, began calling the fortified camp 'my castle' — the terror fixed a new name on his home.

cat-kittens.text: The original two cats brought ashore are dead and buried by his own hand; two tame descendants kept; the rest went wild and eventually had to be shot for plundering the house.

history.value: Lost cat returned in late August with three kittens; cats later multiplied so fast they became a pest and had to be driven off.

cautious-with-strangers.text: Approaches unknown people with cautious goodwill — engages from a distance, reads cues before committing.

nudges.note: Hauled in to speak with African coastal people but stayed in the boat; made signs rather than landing; cautious even when welcoming.

cave-dug.text: Cave fully completed by late December: propped ceiling with posts (which also serve as partitions), shelves fitted, dresser set up, all goods stored inside — functions as warehouse, kitchen, dining-room, and cellar.

history.value: Made a tent from the sail and cut poles; fortified it with a ring of empty chests and casks; slept inside with pistols and gun at hand.

Relocated camp to a hillside site on the N.N.W. side of the hill: a small plain before a hollow rock face, sheltered from the sun, secure above rising ground, with a view to the sea for spotting ships.
Dug a cave behind the tent into the rock face, creating a cellar-like store; raised the floor of the enclosure with the excavated earth.
Camp now has a double tent (inner and outer, covered with tarpaulin) inside the palisade, sleeping in the mate's hammock, with a dug cave behind serving as a cellar.
Cave extended sideways and outward through the rock, creating a separate storehouse room with a back-door exit through the palisade wall.

cedar-canoe-built.text: Built a large cedar periagua — five feet ten inches diameter at the base, hollowed by mallet and chisel over several months — big enough for twenty-six men, but stranded a hundred yards from the water and never launched.

circumnavigation-begun.text: Began the island circumnavigation cruise on 6 November in the sixth year of captivity.

clothes-from-captain.text: Captain clothed Crusoe from head to foot with his own suit, shirts, gloves, shoes, hat and stockings — the first European clothes Crusoe had worn in twenty-seven years; felt unpleasant and awkward at first.

comparative-gratitude.text: Turns hardship into gratitude by comparing downward — looks to those worse off rather than better, and finds comfort in the contrast.

nudges.note: Reflected that mankind would repine less if they compared their condition to those worse off rather than better; this followed directly from the cannibal horror.

conscience-suppression.text: Actively suppresses conscience and reflection when circumstances ease.

nudges.note: Described shaking off serious thoughts 'as from a distemper', mastering conscience through drinking within five or six days of a near-fatal storm.

counts-cost-too-late.text: Prone to beginning ambitious projects before reckoning the full cost — plunges into work then discovers a fatal obstacle too late

nudges.note: Built a huge canoe over months, never considered how to launch it until done — 'the folly of beginning a work before we count the cost'.

crop-defence-methods.text: Defended the crop from beasts with a hedge and dog-guard, and from birds by shooting three and hanging them as scarecrows — birds forsook the area entirely while the scarecrows remained.

crop-enlarged-for-two.text: Marked out and fenced a larger plot to grow enough corn for two mouths — Friday helped willingly and hard.

crusoe-age-at-appeal.text: Was eighteen years old when he appealed to his mother for consent to a sea voyage.

crusoe-birth-name.text: Birth name was Robinson Kreutznaer; anglicised by common usage to Crusoe.

crusoe-birthplace.text: Born in 1632 in the city of York.

crusoe-family-position.text: Third son of the family; two elder brothers, one killed at Dunkirk, the second lost without trace.

crusoe-fears-inquisition.text: Crusoe fears that if he rescues the Spaniards they may betray him to New Spain's Inquisition — prefers being devoured by savages to falling into the Inquisition's hands; he demanded solemn oaths before agreeing to help.

crusoe-jealous-friday.text: Crusoe's jealousy of Friday fully dissolved — repeated probing found nothing but honesty; Friday never perceived the distrust; Crusoe acknowledged he had wronged Friday.

history.value: Friday's visible longing for home made Crusoe jealous and suspicious for several weeks — feared Friday might betray him to his nation and lead a hundred cannibals back; pulled back in warmth; then acknowledged he had wronged Friday and was sorry.

crusoe-married.text: Married during his settled years in England — to his advantage and satisfaction — and had three children: two sons and one daughter.

crusoe-moral-scruple-attack-50.text: On marching toward the savages, Crusoe again reasoned he had no right to attack people who had done him no wrong — resolved to observe and act only if God gave him a clearer call.

crusoe-wary-of-gratitude.text: Crusoe does not assume gratitude is reliable — explicitly articulated that gratitude is no inherent virtue and men act by expected advantage, not obligation; demands oaths and contracts before trusting strangers with his safety.

nudges.note: Stated plainly to the Spaniard: 'gratitude was no inherent virtue in the nature of man'; insisted on sworn contracts before agreeing to rescue the sixteen.

current-heading-gambia.text: Reached and rounded Cape de Verde in the longboat, sighting the Cape de Verde Islands offshore.

history.value: Current plan: sail south to reach the Gambia or Senegal / Cape de Verde and meet a European ship, or perish.

daily-routine.text: Entered the third year with a firm daily order: scripture reading three times daily, morning gun walk, food preparation, and evening work — seldom idle.

history.value: Daily routine from 4 November: morning gun walk (2–3 hrs), work until 11, eat, midday sleep 12–2 (heat), work again in evening.

dairy-set-up.text: Set up a dairy from the goat herd — a gallon or two of milk a day; self-taught butter and cheese making; also found and made salt from sun-evaporated sea water on rocks.

date-concurrences.text: Observed that three pivotal events all shared the same calendar date: left home/enslaved at Sallee; escaped Yarmouth wreck/escaped Sallee; birthday 30 September/cast ashore on the island.

defies-counsel.text: Acts against the advice of those who know better, even when sincerely moved by it.

nudges.note: Was genuinely affected by father's tearful plea, resolved to stay — then abandoned the resolution within days.
In the midst of terror during the storm, Crusoe made solemn vows to return home; within days of the storm passing he drowned all repentance in punch and company.
Despite the master's solemn warning at Yarmouth — and his own admission that reason said go home — Crusoe could not bring himself to return to Hull.
Shame at neighbours prevented going home after the wreck; as the memory of distress faded, so did any inclination to return — he simply waited until the impulse died and looked for a new voyage.

deliverance-arrived.text: Deliverance arrived — the recovered ship rode at anchor half a mile from shore, the captain embraced Crusoe as 'my dear friend and deliverer', and Crusoe saw his escape from the island as finally and visibly in his hands.

departure-date-1659.text: Departed Brazil on 1 September 1659, eight years to the day from first leaving Hull.

dog-companion.text: The ship's dog swam ashore and became a trusty companion for many years on the island; the two cats were also brought ashore.

dog-died-old-age.text: The ship's dog died of old age after sixteen years as a companion on the island.

dried-grapes-method.text: Harvested over 200 bunches of sun-dried grapes as raisins on 3 August — became the main winter food store.

history.value: Hung grapes on outer tree branches to dry in the sun after heap was destroyed by animals — adopted drying method to preserve them as raisins.

drowned-boy-found.text: A few days after the wreck, the corpse of a drowned boy washed ashore — wearing a seaman's waistcoat, open-kneed linen drawers, and blue linen shirt; pockets held two pieces of eight and a tobacco pipe (the pipe far more valued).

earthquake-event.text: A major earthquake struck the island on 17 April: three shocks, cave cracked, large rock fell near the sea, the sea itself disturbed — most terrifying event since the shipwreck.

east-point-rocks-hazard.text: The east side of the island has a ledge of rocks running two leagues out to sea and a sand shoal half a league beyond — a major navigation hazard requiring a wide detour.

english-ship-arrives.text: An English ship appeared at anchor two and a half leagues distant (SSE), with an English long-boat — 11 men came ashore, 3 of them prisoners; Crusoe hidden on secret providential warning that English ships had no good business in these waters.

escape-canoe-not-pursued.text: The four savages who escaped told their nation Crusoe and Friday were heavenly spirits who dart fire — the Caribs believed the island enchanted and never attempted it again.

history.value: The four savages who escaped in the canoe were not successfully pursued — a strong north-west gale arose within two hours, making their survival unlikely; they probably never reached their coast.

escape-plan-reckless-impulse.text: The escape dream from the twenty-fourth year was largely fulfilled in reality — a condemned prisoner ran from cannibals toward him and became his servant — though Crusoe deliberately did not bring him into the grove as in the dream.

history.value: In the twenty-fourth year was seized by an unresisted impulse to sail to the mainland — the plan was wholly reckless (no thought of provision, safe landing, or escape from savages), driven by desperate longing for company after the disappointment at the wreck.

escape-supplies.text: Escaped with: biscuit, three jars of fresh water, beeswax, twine, hatchet, saw, hammer, powder, shot, bottles of liquor, and three fusees.

escape-via-large-boat.text: Friday said Crusoe could reach the mainland in a boat the size of two canoes — a large boat; the first credible escape plan since arriving on the island; raised hope of eventual escape.

faith-shaken-by-fear.text: The footprint fear drove out all former religious confidence — Crusoe noted that fear banished the faith and resignation he had built through years of scripture; compared himself to Saul forsaken.

family-extinct.text: Father dead; mother and all family extinct on return — only two sisters and two nephews of a brother survived; no provision had been left for Crusoe as he had long been presumed dead.

father-counsel-sea.text: Father explicitly forbade the sea and prophesied ruin, saying God would not bless the choice — counsel Crusoe later acknowledges as prophetic.

father-no-assurance.text: After the wreck news reached York, father had no assurances for a long time that Crusoe had not drowned.

father-occupation.text: Father was a Bremen merchant who built a good estate by trade, then retired to York.

fear-makes-worse-than-event.text: Finds that the expectation of evil is more bitter than the actual suffering — anticipatory dread outlasts and surpasses the events feared.

nudges.note: Reflected explicitly that expectation of evil is more bitter than the suffering, after fifteen months of unquiet sleep over savages who did not return.

fear-panic-plans.text: Fear-driven impulse to demolish enclosures, dig up corn-fields, and tear down the bower to erase all traces of habitation — recognized later as irrational; did not act on them.

fever-dream-angel.text: In feverish delirium dreamed of a blazing figure from a black cloud threatening death as punishment for want of repentance.

first-grace-before-meal.text: Ate roasted turtle eggs on 28 June and asked God's blessing before eating — the first time he could remember doing so in his whole life.

first-harvest-yield.text: First successful harvest (late December) yielded roughly two bushels of rice and two and a half bushels of barley from a half-peck of seed — all reserved as seed-corn, none eaten.

first-human-voice.text: Friday spoke words Crusoe could not understand — the first sound of a human voice he had heard, other than his own, in above twenty-five years.

first-prayer-on-island.text: Prayed aloud for the first time since the storm off Hull during the worst of the June fever — helpless, confused, crying 'Lord, look upon me!'

first-salvage-load.text: Final accumulated salvage includes: rigging, ropes, rope-twine, spare canvas, all sails (cut into pieces), cables, hawser, ironwork, sprit-sail yard, mizzen yard, hogshead of bread, three runlets of rum, box of sugar, barrel of fine flour, razors, scissors, ten-to-twelve knives and forks, and about £36 in mixed coin (European, Brazil, pieces of eight, gold, silver).

history.value: First raft load included: bread, rice, three Dutch cheeses, dried goat flesh, corn remnants, cordial waters, rack (5-6 gallons), spare clothing, a carpenter's chest (full), two fowling-pieces, two pistols, powder-horns, bag of shot, two old swords, two barrels of dry powder.
Lacks: ink (none can be made), spade, pickaxe, shovel, needles, pins, thread — these shortages make every task slow and laborious.

first-ship-sank.text: The first ship Crusoe sailed on foundered and sank in Yarmouth Roads during the second storm.

first-shore-party-defeated.text: The two ringleader mutineers were killed or clubbed to death during the first shore attack; three remaining first-party mutineers were taken prisoner and bound hand and foot.

first-shot-on-island.text: Fired his musket in combat for the first time on the island — killed a pursuing savage with one shot to the breast at distance; also knocked another down with the gun-stock.

first-voyage-date.text: First sea voyage departed 1 September 1651 from Hull to London.

five-canoes-feast.text: Five canoes with at least thirty savages landed on his side of the island — the largest group yet; plan to capture one prisoner had relied on a small party; the large number put all prior attack schemes out of reach.

five-trustworthy-recruits.text: Five former mutineers agreed to help retake the ship in exchange for pardon; five others were kept as hostages — their lives hostage to the fidelity of the five going aboard.

five-years-routine.text: Five uneventful years passed after the fourth year in the same routine — annual planting, raisin harvest, daily gun walk — nothing extraordinary occurred.

footprint-discovered.text: Discovered a single print of a naked human foot in the sand near the shore — unmistakable, with toes, heel, and every part; stood paralysed with terror, fled home, slept nothing that night, and could form nothing but dismal imaginations.

force-seven-men.text: Crusoe's fighting force grew to seven well-armed men: Crusoe, Friday, the captain, the mate, the passenger, and two former prisoners who switched sides.

four-years-brazil.text: Had been living in Brazil for nearly four years and had learned the language and made friends among planters and merchants at St. Salvador.

four-years-on-island.text: Completed the fourth year on the island; anniversary kept with devotion; views the world as a remote place he has left behind — 'a great gulf fixed'.

fresh-water-found.text: Found fresh water about a furlong from shore on the first evening.

friday-benamuckee.text: Friday's people worship Benamuckee — an ancient, remote deity older than sea, land, moon, and stars; prayers are relayed through old men (Oowokakee) who climb mountains to speak to him; Crusoe identified this as priestcraft.

friday-cannibal-nature.text: After tasting roast kid, Friday voluntarily declared he would never eat man's flesh again.

history.value: Friday still had a hankering for human flesh and remained cannibal in nature — Crusoe showed such abhorrence that Friday durst not act on it; warned him he would be killed if he did.

friday-courage-battle.text: Friday is cool and deadly under fire — follows orders exactly, aims better than Crusoe, and pursues routed enemies without hesitation.

nudges.note: Battle: outshot Crusoe in first volley, pursued fleeing savages with hatchet and killed most; did not hesitate once ordered.

friday-dislikes-salt.text: Friday found salt repugnant — nauseated and spat at it; would not use salt with meat or broth, at least for a long time.

friday-equal-soul-reflection.text: Reflected with wonder that Friday showed the same reason, affections, gratitude, fidelity, and capacity for good as any European — and was troubled that Providence hid saving knowledge from so many millions of souls; checked the thought: God is just and will judge each by the light given to them.

friday-father-pagan.text: Friday's father is described as a pagan and a cannibal — given liberty of conscience on the island.

friday-father-rescued.text: Friday's father was found bound in the savages' canoe — cut free by Crusoe, revived with rum and water; suffered severe swelling and stiffness from long binding; saved but unable to walk.

friday-filial-affection.text: Friday's love for his father is as fierce as his loyalty to Crusoe — reunion brought him to ecstatic weeping, dancing, and selfless care.

nudges.note: Friday wept, danced, nursed his father's limbs, refused food for himself, sprinted home and back — Crusoe said he could not describe half the extravagances of his affection.

friday-given-gun.text: Taught Friday to shoot and explained gunpowder and bullets; gave him a knife, belt, and hatchet in a frog — fully equipped as a companion and defender.

friday-gun-awe.text: Friday was so awed by the gun that he would not touch it for days — spoke to it privately to beg it not to kill him; believed it had a wonderful fund of death and destruction.

friday-learned-english.text: Friday learned to speak English well enough to hold a full conversation; was the aptest scholar, merry and diligent — Crusoe had genuine use for his tongue again for the first time in twenty-five years.

friday-lodged.text: Friday lodged in a small tent in the space between the two fortifications; Crusoe installed a barred framed door to the inner cave entry and took all weapons inside each night — precautions soon found unnecessary given Friday's loyalty.

friday-longs-for-home.text: Standing on the hilltop, Friday saw his homeland on the mainland and was overwhelmed with joy — dancing, jumping, crying out; his longing to return to his country was vivid and undisguised.

friday-loyalty.text: Friday proved the most faithful, loving, sincere servant imaginable — without passions, sullenness, or designs; his affection to Crusoe like that of a child to a father; would readily sacrifice his life to save Crusoe's.

friday-nation-info.text: Friday's people are the Caribs — their range is from the mouth of the Orinoco to Guiana and on toward St. Martha; they eat captives and Friday himself had feasted on twenty-three people on the northwest shore of the island on a previous visit.

history.value: Friday's nation generally won their battles but he was captured when outnumbered in a particular engagement; his nation took many prisoners in other places; they had no canoe at the time to recover him.

friday-no-fear-beasts.text: Friday had no fear of wild beasts — having known wolves and bears in his own country — and used that familiarity to shoot a wolf at point-blank and sport with a bear where others would have hesitated.

friday-physical-description.text: Friday is about twenty-six years old — well-made and tall, with long black hair, high forehead, bright dark eyes, a round plump face, small nose, thin lips, and white teeth; skin a dun olive-colour; manly yet sweet expression, especially when smiling.

friday-pointed-to-burial.text: On the way to the castle Friday pointed to where he had buried the two pursuers and signed that they should dig them up and eat them — Crusoe showed strong abhorrence; Friday submitted instantly.

friday-religious-instruction.text: Crusoe opened Friday's eyes to the true God, Christ, and prayer; Friday grasped these readily, comparing God to Benamuckee; stumped Crusoe with the question of why God does not kill the devil, then drew his own conclusion: God preserves all to repent and be pardoned.

friday-rescued.text: Rescued a condemned prisoner from a cannibal feast of thirty savages in the twenty-fifth year — the man pledged lifelong service by kneeling and setting Crusoe's foot on his head; Crusoe named him Friday after the day of rescue.

friday-sailor.text: Friday became an expert sailor at the rudder and sail — though he could not be taught the compass; learned quickly once given practical use of the boat.

friday-sword-skill.text: Friday had never seen a metal sword before, yet cut off a man's head cleanly at one blow — apparently accustomed to hard wooden swords sharp and heavy enough to do the same.

friday-teaches-crusoe-scripture.text: Teaching Friday the Scripture forced Crusoe to study things he had never fully considered — Friday's questions made him a much better Scripture scholar than private reading alone would have; grief sat lighter, the habitation grew comfortable beyond measure.

friday-unshakeable-devotion.text: Friday's attachment to Crusoe is unconditional — he will not leave and would rather die than be separated.

nudges.note: Hatchet scene: offered himself to be killed rather than be sent away; tears in his eyes; Crusoe called it the utmost affection.

friday-wants-crusoe-to-missionise.text: Friday's desire to return to his nation was rooted in wanting Crusoe to come and teach them to pray, eat bread, and live well — not in any plan to betray Crusoe.

goat-trapping.text: Tame goat herd fully established from the three trapped kids: 12 goats within 1.5 years, 43 within 3.5 years; five enclosed pastures with gates and drive-pens; goat flesh available whenever wanted.

history.value: In the eleventh year, set pitfall traps and snares to catch live goats; caught one old he-goat and three kids (one male, two female) in a single night.

goatskin-clothing.text: Full island outfit: goatskin cap with rear flap, short goatskin jacket, open-kneed breeches, buskin-like leg-flaps laced at sides, two wide belts (saw and hatchet at sides, powder and shot pouches over shoulder), basket on back, gun on shoulder, goatskin umbrella overhead; long Turkish-style whiskers.

history.value: Made a complete goatskin outfit: cap with hair outward, waistcoat, open-kneed breeches — chosen for coolness and rain-shedding rather than warmth; linen shirts from seamen's chests preserved for the heat.

goods-only-valuable-in-use.text: Came to see that all worldly goods are only good for use — possessed food, timber, grain, fruit in abundance but had no room for covetousness; the £36 coin grew mouldy and worthless.

governor-fiction.text: Crusoe played the role of an unseen English 'governor' of the island with fifty men — a fiction that awed all the mutineers into compliance; he was addressed as 'his excellency'.

grain-crop-started.text: Two failed sowings and one success established the pattern: two rainy seasons per year (March-April and September-October) yield two harvests; sow just before each rainy season.

history.value: Harvested all barley and rice ears (~10–12 barley, ~20–30 rice stalks) for seed; first sowing failed by planting before the dry season; plans to keep sowing until enough for bread.

grateful-generous.text: repays kindness generously — money returned and annuities given unsolicited

nudges.note: Began genuinely to love Friday — said so plainly; content on the island so long as safe from more savages; the warmest human attachment since leaving England.
Crusoe refused to profit from the captain's hardship, returned 60 moidores, released the debt, and settled an annuity — unprompted generosity at the moment of great wealth.

gratitude-generosity.text: Responds to generosity and charity with deep, lasting gratitude.

nudges.note: Offered all he had to the Portuguese captain in gratitude; described his rescue as inexpressible joy.
Upon reaching shore after the surf, first act was to lift his hands and thank God for his life; intense ecstasy at deliverance.

gratitude-settled.text: Has settled into genuine daily gratitude — compares actual condition to what it might have been, and always finds it better than deserved

nudges.note: Spent whole days in lively comparison of actual vs possible-worst; reached sincere thankfulness and resolved never to repine again.

grindstone-wheel.text: Invented a foot-treadle wheel to turn the grindstone, allowing both hands free for tool-grinding — took a week to build.

guinea-captain-dead.text: The Guinea captain died shortly after returning from the first successful Guinea voyage.

guinea-captain-honest.text: The Guinea captain was honest, plain-dealing, and acted with disinterested honesty in Crusoe's investment.

guinea-voyage-decision.text: Agreed to sail as supercargo on a secret Guinea slave-trading voyage, abandoning his plantation after nearly four years of prospering there.

guinea-voyage-profit.text: First Guinea voyage profit: £40 invested in trifles yielded almost £300 from gold-dust — his only profitable voyage.

initial-inventory-nothing.text: Upon landing had no clothes to change, no food, no drink, no weapons — only a knife, tobacco-pipe, and a little tobacco.

ink-running-low.text: Ink finally gone — eked to transparency with water; journal use ended except for the most remarkable events.

history.value: Ink began to fail after one year on the island; resolved to write only the most remarkable events, not a daily memorandum.

inner-cave-found.text: Found a natural cave in the interior woods: a small outer chamber (~12 ft across) leading through a low ten-yard crawl to a vast inner vault with a twenty-foot ceiling, dry gravel floor, no damp, and walls that reflected candlelight in a hundred thousand lights.

island-colony-stocked.text: Sent further settlers from Brazil to the island: seven women, five cows (three in calf), sheep, and hogs — the colony growing and self-sustaining.

island-confirmed.text: Confirmed from a hilltop that the location is an island, surrounded entirely by sea — barren, uninhabited, with only wild beasts and unknown birds.

island-contentment.text: Finds the solitary island life genuinely happier than the wicked life that preceded it — spiritual gain outweighs physical misery

nudges.note: Second anniversary reflection: sensibly felt the island life was happier than all past wicked days; desires and affections wholly changed.

island-currents-noted.text: Observed strong opposing currents on both the south and north sides of the island that meet in the island's wake; a counter-eddy on the north-east caused by offshore rocks offered a return path.

island-departure-date.text: Left the island on 19 December 1686 after twenty-eight years, two months, and nineteen days — the same day of the month as his escape from the Moors of Sallee.

island-fever.text: Fever and ague broken by 3 July after tobacco-rum treatment; strength gradually restored over several weeks.

history.value: Struck by a severe fever and ague from about 19 June — violent headaches, chills, seven-hour ague fit, too weak to stand or fetch water.

island-fifteen-years.text: Now fifteen years on the island and had not met any person in all that time before the footprint.

island-geography.text: Island has a high central hill overtopping a ridge running northward; two small islands lie about three leagues to the west; no visible land except some distant rocks.

island-grief-lifting.text: The sudden fits of anguish — wringing hands and weeping over being a prisoner locked in an ocean wilderness — have given way to new thoughts drawn from daily scripture; sorrows and joys both changed.

island-history-told-captain.text: Crusoe told the captain his complete twenty-seven-year island history; the captain was moved to tears and believed Crusoe had been providentially preserved to save him.

island-interior-explored.text: Explored interior from 15 July: creek runs two miles inland (tidal limit), flanked by savannahs; valley beyond the woods described as a planted garden with cocoa, orange, lemon, citron trees.

island-land-divided.text: Divided the island into portions among the settlers, reserving overall ownership to himself; engaged them formally not to leave the place.

island-latitude.text: Reckoned by observation to be at latitude 9 degrees 22 minutes north of the equator.

island-location-orinoco.text: Confirmed from Friday's knowledge that the island lies in the mouth or gulf of the Orinoco; the land to the west and northwest is the island of Trinidad, at the north point of the Orinoco's mouth.

island-name.text: Named the island 'The Island of Despair' in the journal on 30 September 1659.

island-population-four.text: The island now has four inhabitants: Crusoe, Friday, Friday's father, and the Spaniard — Crusoe jokingly considers himself king over subjects of three religions.

island-revisited-1694.text: Revisited the island in 1694 on the East Indies voyage — found the Spaniards and mutineers there, learned their history of conflict and Caribbean battles; stayed twenty days; divided the land and left supplies including two English workmen.

island-seen-as-beloved-home.text: When swept out to sea, called the island his 'beloved island' and 'happy desert' — desire to return was overwhelming; the island is now felt as home.

island-ten-months.text: Had now been on the island above ten months as of 15 July; firmly believed no human had ever set foot there.

island-wildlife.text: A lamed goat nursed back to health and grown tame — grazes by the door; first step toward a tame animal herd for food after powder runs out.

history.value: Island has abundance of unknown fowls; a hawk-like bird shot proved carrion; a tame wild-cat-like creature visited the camp and ate offered biscuit.
Island has wild goats; they are wary but can be hunted from above on rocks — first shot killed a she-goat; kid attempted as first taming effort, failed.
Island wildlife observed: wild goats, ducks, unknown edible birds, wild cat (skin kept), seals on the shore, many sea-fowls.

killing-savages-scruple.text: Heart trembled at shedding human blood for his deliverance — for a long time could not reconcile killing savages even in self-defence; the desire for deliverance eventually prevailed over the scruple.

labour-patience.text: Carries through any task by patient, relentless labour however long it takes — never abandons a necessity for want of proper tools

nudges.note: Forty-two days on one shelf board, three months fencing and sowing, constant improvisation — 'labour and patience carried me through'.

land-sighted-west.text: Sighted high land to the W/WSW from the island's western shore — estimated 15-20 leagues distant; concluded it must be part of America, either Spanish dominions or the savage coast between Spanish territory and Brazil.

landing-date.text: First set foot on the island on 30 September 1659 — recorded on a post-cross erected at the landing spot.

large-canoe-built.text: A large periagua (fustic-like timber) was built by Crusoe and Friday over about six weeks — capable of carrying twenty men; fitted with a cedar mast, a shoulder-of-mutton sail from old canvas, anchor, and cable.

large-planks-cut.text: Cut about a dozen large oak planks (30-35 ft long, 2-4 inches thick) — preliminary work toward building a vessel for the escape.

leopard-skin-acquired.text: Acquired a fine spotted leopard skin from the African coastal people after shooting the leopard.

lisbon-procuration-filed.text: Crusoe registered an affidavit of being alive with a Lisbon notary and sent a procuration to Brazil authorising the Portuguese captain to receive annual plantation profits on his behalf.

living-stake-hedge.text: Bower stakes sprouted into trees forming a full canopy; planted a double row of living stakes as outer hedge around the main camp wall — grew into a dense, defensive screen.

longboat-staved.text: The first longboat was staved — a hole knocked in her bottom too big to be quickly stopped — to prevent the remaining 26-man ship's crew from reclaiming her.

longing-for-companion.text: At the sight of the wreck, felt the strongest desire for human company he had ever known — wished desperately that even one survivor had been saved; his hands clenched and teeth ground involuntarily from the force of the longing.

lost-day-reckoning.text: After the long tobacco-rum sleep lost one day in his calendar reckoning — never recovered which day it was; calendar is now one day off.

mainland-escape-desire.text: Abandoned the plan to cross to the mainland — the small canoe is too small for the forty-mile crossing; island circumnavigation is the new aim.

history.value: Persistently drawn toward the mainland visible to the west, hoping to escape — aware that Caribbean coast people may be cannibals but the desire overrides caution.

mainland-escape-plan-active.text: Crusoe fixed on a plan to cross to the continent with Friday to join the seventeen bearded men — almost certainly Spaniards or Portuguese — believing escape from the continent as a group was more practical than from the island alone.

mortar-pestle-made.text: Carved a wooden mortar by the Indian canoe method (axe, hatchet, fire) and made an iron-wood pestle — will be used to pound corn into meal at the next harvest.

mutineers-no-firearms.text: The mutineers had only two firearms, one of which they left in the boat — they were effectively unarmed on shore.

mutineers-two-ringleaders.text: The captain warned there were two particularly desperate villains among the mutineers whom it was scarce safe to show mercy to — the rest would return to duty if those two were secured.

nephews-in-care.text: Took in his two nephews — bred the elder as a gentleman, placed the younger with a sea-captain; the younger eventually drew Crusoe himself back into further adventures.

no-compass-on-canoe.text: Had no compass aboard the canoe — was wholly dependent on keeping the island in sight to find his way back.

not-satisfied-with-station.text: Repeatedly fails to remain content in a settled, prosperous station — defies God and nature by seeking change when he has everything he needs.

nudges.note: Explicitly named restless wandering the 'original sin' and 'plague of mankind' — calculated would be worth 100,000 moidores if he had stayed in Brazil.

obey-inner-dictates.text: Follows inner providential nudges as a firm rule, trusting inward impressions over visible logic.

nudges.note: After reflecting on unseen deliverances, adopted a personal rule to always obey secret hints or pressings of mind — never to slight them.

original-sin-named.text: Named his repeated defiance of Providence as his 'original sin' — the failure to be content with the Brazilian plantation was the direct cause of the island; calculates he might have been worth 100,000 moidores had he stayed.

osier-grove-planted.text: Planted roughly 20,000 osier stakes between the outer wall and the surrounding land — grew into an impenetrable wood in five or six years, making all trace of habitation invisible.

oven-made.text: Improvised a working oven: a tile-paved hearth heated with embers, loaves covered by an inverted earthen pot with embers raked around it — bakes barley loaves and rice cakes well.

palisade-fortification.text: Outer perimeter wall completed 14 April: a 24-yard half-circle of double piles with turf wall, so well disguised the camp is invisible from the shore.

history.value: Erected a double-row palisade of sharpened stakes with cable fill around the new camp entrance — no door, only a ladder lifted over from inside — forming a secure enclosure impenetrable to man or beast.

parrot-caught.text: Taught the parrot to say 'Poll' — the first word spoken on the island by any mouth but his own.

history.value: Caught a young parrot on the western expedition; years later taught it to call him by name.

past-fear-in-desperation.text: acts with calm courage when circumstances are already desperate — sees mortal risk as deliverance either way and refuses to be paralysed by fear

nudges.note: Told the captain men in their circumstances were past the operation of fear, smiling at his terror of the second armed boat.

perspective-glass-plan.text: Resolved after spotting a possible boat at sea never to go out without his perspective glass — had left it behind this time.

plantation-alien-nature.text: Crusoe found plantation life quite contrary to his nature — he had entered an employment remote from his genius and directly opposed to the wandering life he desired.

plantation-income-received.text: Brazil plantation accounts arrived: 1,174 moidores (first 6 years), 3,240 moidores (next 4 years), 872 moidores (Prior of St Augustine), plus 1,200 chests of sugar, 800 rolls of tobacco, and remainder in gold.

plantation-prospering.text: Left the plantation in the care of the three merchant partners; formal will made naming the Portuguese captain as universal heir.

history.value: After the English-goods cargo arrived, Crusoe quadrupled his investment and bought a slave and servant; plantation was prospering and growing.

pleasantest-year.text: The three years Crusoe and Friday lived together were perfectly and completely happy — Friday became a good Christian, the habitation felt comfortable, and religious discussion filled their days.

history.value: The year after Friday's arrival was the pleasantest of all years on the island — language, company, and real affection; no longer desolate.

poll-found-at-bower.text: Poll the parrot had made his way to the bower and greeted Crusoe there with his own taught phrases — a source of surprised comfort after the ordeal.

poll-parrot-age.text: Poll the parrot lived with Crusoe no less than twenty-six years in all; spoke articulately and plainly — the best of all his parrots.

portuguese-captain-annuity.text: Crusoe granted the Portuguese captain 100 moidores per year for life and his son 50 moidores per year after him, as reward for decades of honesty and kindness.

portuguese-captain-charity.text: The Portuguese captain refused any reward and pledged to carry Crusoe to Brazil on charity, keeping all his goods safe.

portuguese-captain-debt.text: Portuguese captain owed Crusoe 470 moidores from plantation profits he received, plus lost 60 chests of sugar and 15 rolls of tobacco in his own shipwreck — released from debt by Crusoe's gift.

potter-wheel-made.text: Fashioned a potter's wheel, producing round, well-shaped earthenware — a significant improvement over the crude hand-formed pots made earlier.

pottery-plan.text: Mastered fire-hardening of clay pots using a slow kiln built from firewood and embers; now has earthenware sufficient for all needs, including fire-bearing cooking vessels, one partially glazed.

history.value: Resolved to make sun-dried clay pots to solve the vessel shortage — needed for storing dry grain and meal.

powder-running-low.text: Gunpowder store now reduced to within the quantity of one barrel — a critical constraint on any plan to use explosives or fire regularly.

history.value: By the eleventh year, the gunpowder stock had abated considerably — not replenishable, a growing concern for hunting goats.

practical-ingenuity.text: solves practical problems through patient improvisation rather than giving up

nudges.note: Spent a full week inventing a foot-treadle grindstone wheel from scratch with no prior knowledge — devoted as much thought to it as a statesman to politics.
Drew on childhood basket-making observation to master wicker-work from scratch — a skill absorbed at seven applied thirty years later under necessity.

pre-island-irreligion.text: The seafaring life laughed out all religious sense — through Sallee, rescue, Brazil, and all earlier deliverances he never once said 'Thank God'; father and mother's religious instruction was wholly abandoned.

priestcraft-observation.text: Observed that making religion secret to preserve clerical veneration is universal — found among the most brutish savages just as in Roman and all other religions.

providence-ignorance-reflection.text: Reflected that Providence mercifully bounds human sight — a man walks amid countless dangers he cannot see and is kept serene by ignorance; if he could see them all, his mind would be overwhelmed.

providence-reasoning.text: Sitting by the calm sea on 28 June, reasoned unprompted from the visible world to a Creator who must guide and govern all things — the first natural-theology reflection of his life.

rainy-season-danger.text: Learned from the fever that going abroad in rainy-season storms is the most dangerous thing to health on the island.

rational-planner.text: Plans shelter and security systematically, weighing multiple criteria before committing to a course of action.

nudges.note: Enumerated four explicit criteria (health/water, shade, security, sea view) before choosing the new camp site, then engineered the palisade with care.
Drew a formal written 'debtor and creditor' account of his condition to master despondency; organised cave with shelves and tools by category.

rebel-captain-killed.text: The rebel captain (new captain of the mutinied ship) was shot through the head by the mate in the round-house — the only death in the ship's recapture.

relics-taken.text: Took as relics on departure: the goatskin cap, the umbrella, one of the parrots, and both stores of coin (the island silver and the Spanish wreck money).

religious-awakening-under-extremity.text: turns to God and prayer only under mortal extremity, not in ordinary hardship

nudges.note: First prayer since the Hull storm only came when he was too weak to stand, near death from fever — not during years of routine island hardship.
Acknowledges himself that conscience slept through years of slavery, storms, and shipwreck — it only awoke when fever brought him face to face with dying alone.
After recovery begins reading the Bible daily and praying regularly — the pattern is shifting: what began as crisis prayer is becoming a practice.
Daily Bible reading and prayer now continued in recovery and health — the practice has moved well beyond crisis.

religious-calm-suspended.text: All calm of mind and resignation to Providence was suspended by the overpowering escape impulse — as if he had no power to turn his thoughts to anything else.

religious-rationaliser.text: When despair strikes, wrestles with Providence and eventually reasons himself back to cautious gratitude by counting advantages against losses.

nudges.note: Wept about his desolate condition and questioned God, then deliberately weighed the good (salvaged goods, life spared) against the bad and recovered equilibrium.
When barley sprouted unexpectedly, immediately interpreted it as a divine miracle and for the first time felt genuine religious stirring — prior to this had lived on no religious foundation.

When the barley's natural origin became clear, his religious thankfulness immediately faded — he confesses faith rises and falls with his understanding of events rather than reflecting a settled conviction.

repentance-ecstasy.text: Worked his mind to genuine thankfulness for Providence — the island is well supplied, punishment is less than deserved, repentance likely accepted, no predators, no savages, no poisons; resolved never to repine again.

history.value: Reading 'He is exalted a Prince and a Saviour to give repentance', threw down the Bible in ecstatic joy and cried aloud for repentance — the first prayer with a true sense of condition and hope.
Came to see deliverance from guilt as the greater blessing — the island's solitude ceased to weigh on him; inner peace established through daily Bible reading and prayer.

rescue-deferred-harvest.text: After the expanded harvest (220+ bushels barley, proportionate rice), food stores are now sufficient to provision all sixteen Spaniards and victualling a vessel for any American voyage.

history.value: Plan to fetch the sixteen Europeans deferred at least half a year on the Spaniard's advice — food stores insufficient for twenty people and a sea voyage; will wait for the next harvest and expand cultivation first.

rescued-by-portuguese-ship.text: Rescued from the longboat by a Portuguese ship; taken aboard with all goods; ship bound toward Brazil.

resigned-contentment.text: Lives in a state of settled, composed contentment — resigning all to God's providence turns solitude into something better than sociable

nudges.note: Described living 'mighty comfortably', mind entirely composed by resignation to providence; found conversing with God better than human society.

resolve-go-england.text: Resolved to go to England rather than Brazil, unable to find a trustworthy keeper for his wealth — the plantation management delegated to the Portuguese captain via procuration.

resourceful-under-necessity.text: Acts with relentless practical resourcefulness under mortal necessity — exhausting every option before conceding defeat.

nudges.note: Made eleven salvage trips over thirteen days, recovering even ironwork by diving, and reflected with calm satisfaction that he had wasted no time when the ship was finally lost.
When lacking a shovel, found iron-tree wood and spent days laboriously shaping a working wooden one.
After the earthquake, while terrified, methodically cut a drainage hole to prevent flooding and immediately began planning a second camp rather than giving up.

revenge-mood-renewed.text: After seeing the cannibal remains, fell back into a murdering humour — spent months planning to attack savages on their next visit, dreaming of killing them at night; apprehension made him sleep unquietly for fifteen months.

sabbath-observance.text: Set aside every seventh day as Sabbath after the anniversary; noted the calendar was a day or two short — calendar now formalised with weekly Sabbath marks.

safety-reasoning.text: Reasoned that the cannibals came to the island by chance and never searched it — having been concealed eighteen years, he could stay concealed eighteen more by staying hidden.

salvage-complete.text: Salvage from the wreck is complete; after eleven trips the ship broke up in a storm and disappeared — only debris may yet wash ashore.

salvaged-books-instruments.text: Salvaged from the ship: pens, ink, paper, compasses, mathematical instruments, charts and navigation books, three English Bibles, Portuguese books and prayer-books.

savage-tide-pattern.text: Observed that savages always arrive with the ebb current and depart on the flood — can safely go abroad during flood tide when they are not already ashore.

savages-concluded.text: Concluded the footprint was left by mainland savages blown to the island in canoes — they came and went; the chief fear is they may return in greater numbers.

savages-on-my-side.text: Savages came to his side of the island for the first time — nine of them with two canoes, feasting in December of the twenty-third year; left on the flood tide; no more sightings for fifteen months after.

scruple-overcome-by-christian-prisoner.text: Crusoe's scruple about attacking innocent savages was overcome when he saw a European Christian about to be killed — sight of the bound white man gave him the 'call' he had said he needed.

sea-aversion-overland.text: Had a strong aversion to travelling home by sea — two ships he selected both miscarried — resolved to travel overland through Spain and France to England.

seasonal-calendar.text: Two rainy seasons (mid-Feb to mid-Apr; mid-Aug to mid-Oct) and two dry seasons per year; rain can hold longer or shorter with the winds.

second-anniversary-fast.text: Kept 30 September as a solemn day of humble thanksgiving on the second anniversary of landing; now clearly two years on the island.

second-boat-captured.text: The second longboat was seized — two guards surprised and taken, one of them defecting to Crusoe's side; seven-man search party stranded in the woods after dark, unable to return to the boat.

second-boat-launched.text: The ship launched a second boat with ten armed men toward shore after the first boat did not return — three of the ten were said to be honest men coerced into the conspiracy.

second-camp-plan.text: Now has two permanent habitations: the main fortified cave-camp (enlarged into several inner caves, pots and grain baskets stored in the driest; palisade stakes grown into a dense tree-wall hiding it from view) and the bower country seat (couch inside, sail-tent, enclosure of grown trees) with the goat pastures adjoining.

history.value: Planning a second open-ground camp as an earthquake-safe alternative; resolved 21 April to stay in the cave until it is built — fears being buried alive.
Decided not to remove habitation to the pleasant interior valley — staying near the sea preserves chance of rescue; built a country bower as secondary residence instead.

second-canoe-planned.text: Resolved to build a second periagua for the south side of the island, keeping the north-shore canoe where it is — prefers more labour over more risk.

second-harvest-yield.text: Fixed annual sowing at the same quantity as the second season — forty bushels total is sufficient for bread for one person; will sow once a year.

history.value: Second corn harvest yielded about twenty bushels of barley and as much or more rice — now enough to eat freely; resolved to sow once a year only.

second-voyage-capital.text: Carried under £100 on the second Guinea voyage; left £200 lodged with the first captain's widow.

secret-goat-enclosure.text: Made a second hidden three-acre goat enclosure in the interior woods — ten young she-goats and two he-goats moved there as a backup herd against loss of the main flock.

secret-hints-rule.text: Adopted a firm personal rule to obey secret impressions or inward pressings of mind — interpreted these as providential guidance; resolved never to disregard such hints regardless of visible reason.

self-blamed-folly.text: Prone to looking back with regret and blaming his own obstinacy for his misfortunes.

nudges.note: Calls himself 'the wilful agent of all my own miseries' and preemptively notes he will have leisure to reflect on his miscarriages in future sorrows.
Calls himself 'born to be my own destroyer'; notes he was 'hurried on, obeyed blindly the dictates of my fancy'; preemptively regrets the decision even before setting sail.

self-condemnation-pattern.text: prone to searing self-condemnation in hindsight, judging past self as wicked and hardened

nudges.note: Uses language like 'most hardened, unthinking, wicked creature' and 'uncommon wickedness' to describe the pre-island self; father's prophecy is now a standing weight.

self-taught-craftsman.text: Teaches himself mechanical arts through labour, application, and contrivance — having never handled a tool, eventually masters what he needs.

nudges.note: Made table, chair, and shelves with only adze and hatchet; hewed planks from whole trees; reflected that reason makes a man master of every mechanic art.

seven-man-party-stranded.text: The seven-man search party was lured deep into the island's woods by the hallooing stratagem; they were stranded there after dark, cut off from the second boat.

seventeen-white-men.text: Friday said his nation rescued seventeen white men from a wrecked boat driven ashore on their coast; those men had been living peacefully among the Caribs for about four years — almost certainly survivors of the Spanish wreck Crusoe saw.

shelf-board-labour.text: Took forty-two days to make a single cave shelf-board for want of tools, help, and skill — an index of how grossly want of tools multiplies labour on the island.

ship-recovered.text: The English ship was recovered at midnight: the rebel captain shot dead in the round-house, the rest surrendered; the captain fired seven guns as the agreed signal of success.

ship-reward.text: Ship owners presented Crusoe with almost £200 sterling as reward for saving the ship and crew.

ship-wrecked-near-orinoco.text: Ship was disabled by a twelve-day tornado, driven to near the Guiana coast west of the Amazon and Orinoco, then wrecked on a sandbank after a second storm.

ships-boat-failed.text: The ship's boat lay upturned on the beach; three to four weeks of effort with levers and digging failed to right or move it — abandoned as impossible alone.

sieves-made.text: Made three sieves from calico and muslin neckcloths from the salvaged seamen's clothes — sufficient for sifting meal from bran for several years.

signal-fire-lit.text: On 16 May of year twenty-four, heard two cannon shots at sea during a storm and immediately lit a large signal fire on the hilltop, maintaining it all night; by dawn saw a distant shape far to the east.

sisters-payment.text: Sent each of his two sisters 100 pounds — one a widow, the other in an unhappy marriage, neither in want but not prospering.

slavery-sallee.text: Escaped Moorish slavery at Sallee by sea in the master's longboat, with Xury.

history.value: Enslaved at Sallee by a Moorish rover captain for approximately two years, kept as personal household and ship-watch slave.

sole-survivor.text: Crusoe was the sole survivor of the shipwreck; all other crewmates perished in the surf.

solitude-as-privation.text: Feels the absence of human society as a deep, embodied privation — not just a hardship but a longing that overtakes the body.

nudges.note: The sight of the shipwreck produced the strongest craving for a companion he had ever felt — hands clenched, teeth ground involuntarily.

spaniard-brave.text: The Spaniard fought with remarkable courage despite his emaciated condition — cut two savages in pieces with the sword, shot a third with Crusoe's pistol when being overpowered.

spaniard-oath-allegiance.text: The Spaniard swore a personal oath of allegiance to Crusoe — to remain at his side as long as he lived, take his side to the last drop of his blood, and bring his countrymen under solemn oath to follow Crusoe's orders entirely.

spaniard-rescued.text: A Spaniard (one of the seventeen white bearded men from Friday's account) was rescued from a cannibal feast — hands and feet bound with rushes on the beach; Crusoe cut him free and armed him.

spaniard-sent-to-mainland.text: The Spaniard and Friday's father departed in October in a canoe to fetch the sixteen Europeans — each armed with a musket and 8 charges; provisioned for 8 days; signalling agreed for return.

spaniards-to-west.text: Friday said white bearded men lived beyond the setting moon to the west — Crusoe identified these as Spaniards, whose cruelties were remembered by all the Carib nations from father to son.

spanish-ship-wreck.text: A ship was driven onto the concealed offshore rocks near the south point in a storm on 16 May of year twenty-four — the same rocks that caused the counter-eddy that saved Crusoe from being lost at sea; no survivors seen.

sudden-wealth.text: Suddenly master of above £5,000 sterling in cash and an estate in Brazil worth above £1,000 per year — wealth he scarce knew how to understand.

survival-presence.text: Keeps presence of mind under extreme mortal danger — acts purposefully even when near death.

nudges.note: Methodically deceived the Moor into fetching supplies, loaded the boat under pretence, then executed the escape cleanly — all improvised on the spot.
Shot the lion methodically with three guns, skinned it to recover value from spent shot, improvised fresh water from tidal creek — consistent practical problem-solving throughout the coastal voyage.
In the waves, held breath, swam toward shore, gripped the rock, timed the wave retreats — managed fear with methodical action throughout the surf ordeal.
Built a raft from ship's spars alone, prioritised tools and arms over gold, used the tidal current to navigate back to shore — methodical and practical throughout.
Methodically planned the second salvage, made tent and fortification, resolved to take everything from the wreck before the first storm destroyed it.

swept-out-to-sea.text: While rounding the east point the canoe was seized by a violent current and carried almost two leagues out to sea — a near-fatal incident from which he barely escaped.

tame-household-animals.text: Keeps two or three household kids taught to feed from his hand, two more parrots that call 'Robin Crusoe', and several tame sea-fowl with clipped wings living in the grove before the castle wall.

tame-kid-goat.text: The tame she-goat raised from a kid (captured in the third year) died of old age before he could get a he-goat to breed with her — first attempt at domestic goat breeding came to nothing.

history.value: Captured a young kid on the return journey; it became fully tame after being nursed with food and now lives at the main camp as a domestic animal — the start of a planned tame-goat breeding stock.

taming-pigeons.text: Found wild pigeons nesting in rock holes; raised young ones but they flew away when grown; gathers squabs for food from nests regularly.

temperament/practical.text: Solves practical problems through patient improvisation; acts with relentless resourcefulness under necessity; cautious with strangers; plans shelter and security systematically; self-taught craftsman.

nudges.note: Kept his head under mortal threat — paddled hard to stay near the eddy edge, read the water clarity to detect the current shift, and used every tool (umbrella as awning, salvaged grappling as anchor) to manage the situation.
Invented a potter's wheel, mastered wicker-work, made a clay pipe, and devised pitfall traps for goats — continuous self-taught craftsmanship in the eleventh year.
Recognized and corrected the folly of a two-mile goat enclosure before wasting too much effort; systematically expanded pastures as the herd grew; self-taught dairy-making from first principles.
Observed and correctly diagnosed the tidal origin of the east-point current through patient watching; chose the more laborious but safer option of building a second canoe rather than risk the tide.
Under extreme fear became irrational — nearly acted to demolish his own enclosures and corn; had to talk himself back from disastrous practical decisions.
Stepped back from panic and built a rational, graduated defence system: double wall, musket-cannon, twenty thousand stakes, a secret backup herd — all measured against actual probability of danger.

Acted with precise tactical judgment: descended with two guns, intercepted pursuers without firing unnecessarily (used gun-stock first to avoid noise), then directed Friday to bury the bodies to conceal signs of the encounter.

temperament/religion.text: Conscience opened on the island; now earnestly repentant and daily thankful; instructing Friday deepened his own faith and turned the habitation from an affliction into a joy.

nudges.note: Adrift and nearly lost, immediately turned to providence — saw the incident as God making a miserable condition worse; reproached himself for repining at his solitary state.
First act on reaching shore was to kneel and thank God; spent the next year fully resigned to Providence and composed in his condition.
Fear completely drove out his hard-won religious resignation — he noted the failure himself; only the direct intervention of a scripture verse recalled him to prayer.
Two years of savage-dread have degraded prayer from calm resignation to fearful petition — a sustained setback to the religious composure he had built in earlier years.
Friday's faithfulness and natural goodness prompted deep providential reflection — wondered at God hiding saving knowledge from so many, then checked himself: God judges by the light given to each.

Teaching Friday forced deeper Scripture study; Crusoe concluded he was brought to the island partly to save this man's soul — a secret joy ran through every part of his soul; continued in that thankful frame all the remainder of his time.

three-canoes-savages.text: In the battle: 17 of 21 savages killed (Crusoe, Friday, and the Spaniard all contributing), 4 escaped in the canoe — one of the canoe escapees was wounded and may have died.

history.value: Three canoes of savages arrived — twenty-one savages with three prisoners; they landed near the creek where the wood came close to shore.

three-men-left-on-island.text: Three mutineers were left on the island by choice, given firearms, ammunition, directions on farming, goat husbandry, and tools; told to expect the seventeen Spaniards and to treat them well; Crusoe promised to try to send a vessel for them.

three-years-corn-plan.text: Resolved to sow enough corn to have two or three years' supply in advance, rather than just enough for the next season — the footprint fear made the risk of losing a crop feel real.

tobacco-medicine.text: Used tobacco as medicine against the ague: chewed it, steeped it in rum to drink, and burned it over coals — the tobacco-rum sleeping draught produced a near-two-day sleep that broke the fever.

tobacco-pipe-made.text: Made a clay tobacco-pipe — ugly and clumsy, but hard, firm, and functional; the achievement that gave him the most personal satisfaction of any he had made on the island.

turtle-found.text: First turtle found on the shore 16 June; cooked 17 June — yielded sixty eggs; most savoury meal since landing.

twenty-seventh-year.text: Crusoe entered his twenty-seventh year of captivity on the island — though he counted the three years with Friday as a different kind of life altogether.

twenty-six-hands-aboard.text: Twenty-six hands remained aboard the ship — all having forfeited their lives to the law by the mutiny, making them desperate fighters unlikely to surrender.

twenty-third-year.text: Now in the twenty-fourth year of residence on the island — the encounter with savages on his side was in year twenty-three; a new strange encounter came in May of year twenty-four.

history.value: Now in the twenty-third year of residence on the island — so naturalised he could have been content to remain forever, were it not for the dread of savages.

two-more-years.text: Lived nearly two more years after the wreck salvage in much the same manner — more vigilant, confining movement to the east side; head filled with escape projects but no plan carried out.

two-prisoners-island-option.text: Crusoe maneuvered the two most incorrigible prisoners into requesting to be left on the island rather than taken to England in irons — they feared hanging if transported.

two-years-confined.text: After discovering the cannibal site, confined himself strictly to his three enclosures for almost two years — did not fire his gun once and carried two pistols and a cutlass whenever abroad.

umbrella-made.text: Built a collapsible goatskin umbrella — skin hair-outward repels rain; folds and carries under arm; the best protection he has against sun and rain when out.

wandering-restlessness.text: Has a deep, persistent inclination to wander rather than settle — grows restless and dissatisfied with a quiet, prosperous life.

nudges.note: Head filled early with rambling thoughts; defied both parents' commands and entreaties to pursue the sea.
After the first shipwreck, still refused to go home and headed to London, openly acknowledging an 'ill fate' pushing him forward with unstoppable obstinacy.
After the first profitable Guinea voyage, immediately resolved to repeat it despite the captain's death; the good fortune only inflamed aspiring thoughts that 'have since completed my ruin'.
Explicitly says plantation life was contrary to his genius; calls himself the wilful agent of his own miseries through his inclination to wander; notes he could have stayed in England to do this.

Explicitly chose a risky Guinea voyage over a prospering plantation, calling himself 'born to be my own destroyer' and comparing it to disobeying his father; sailed on an 'evil hour' of his own making.
Despite understanding the current was manageable, terror of the sea kept him from acting on the knowledge — fear now restrains the old wandering impulse.
In the twenty-fourth year the escape impulse overwhelmed religious resignation and all prudent reflection — he couldn't resist the impetuosity of desire even knowing the plan was reckless.
Even after great wealth and seven years held back by the widow, the island and further adventures still called him — nephew lured him back to sea.
Even after marriage, children, and seven years settled, wife's death and nephew's importunity drew him back to sea in 1694 — the pattern confirmed.

wet-powder-recovered.text: Opened the sea-wet barrel and found water had only penetrated 3-4 inches, caking into a protective shell — the inner core yielded about 60 pounds of good dry powder.

wicker-baskets-improved.text: Made an abundance of wicker baskets in various sizes — used for carrying game, eggs, and storing grain after threshing.

widow-dissuades-travel.text: Sailed as private trader to the East Indies with his nephew in 1694 — the resumption of a wandering life after seven years settled in England.

history.value: The widow dissuaded Crusoe from returning abroad for almost seven years — the longest he stayed still after the island.

wife-died.text: Wife died, ending the settled period; nephew's return and importunity then drew Crusoe back to sea.

wild-plants-discovered.text: Found wild tobacco (large stalks), aloes, imperfect sugar cane, melons, abundant grapes on vines, green limes, lemons, cocoa, orange, and citron trees in the island interior — no cassava.

will-atkins-ringleader.text: Will Atkins was the first man to lay hands on the captain during the mutiny and used him barbarously — singled out as the worst and threatened with hanging to extract compliance from the rest.

wolf-battle-gascony.text: Fought off a pack of about a hundred wolves in the Gascony plain by firing alternating volleys and shouting — four wolves killed, the rest driven off; then pushed through wolf-surrounded terrain to reach the village.

world-view-detached.text: By the fourth year, through constant scripture study, the world has become remote — no expectations from it, no desires about it; views it as a place he once lived in but has come out of.

wreck-dog-rescued.text: Rescued a starving dog from the Spanish wreck — nearly dead with hunger and thirst; revived with bread and water; brought home.

wreck-salvage-done.text: Salvaged from the Spanish wreck: two chests (cordial waters, sweetmeats, shirts, linen, ~1,100 pieces of eight, 6 gold doubloons, ~1 lb gold bars, 2 lb glazed powder, shoes), a cask of poor-quality rum, a powder-horn with 4 lb powder, fire-shovel, tongs, two brass kettles, a copper chocolate-pot, and a live dog.

wreck-second-salvage-lumber.text: Worked the broken wreck from May 3 to June 15, recovering enough timber, planks, and ironwork to have built a boat, plus nearly a hundredweight of sheet lead.

wreck-voyage-planned.text: Resolved to sail to the wreck in the canoe — provisioned with bread, water, rum, raisins, rice, barley cakes, milk, cheese, umbrella, and compass; felt the impression to go was providential and irresistible.

xury-faithful.text: Xury swore faithfulness and proved willing and cheerful during the escape voyage.

xury-sold.text: Xury was sold to the Portuguese captain for 60 pieces of eight, with a written promise of freedom in ten years on turning Christian.

xury-sold-regret.text: Crusoe later felt he had done wrong in parting with Xury, whose help was sorely missed on the plantation.

year-of-sedate-life.text: Spent nearly a year after the ocean scare in a sedate, retired, and contented life — composed and resigned to Providence, happy in all things except society.
